title: US interest rates held steady and economy grows - what it means for you
summary: The Federal Reserve's interest rate decisions affect everything from mortgages to car loans
paragraphs: US interest rates held steady and economy grows - what it means for you
The US Federal Reserve has held interest rates steady at 3.75% - 4%.
The decision comes within a week of the midterm elections and after the central bank raised interest rates for the first time in three years at its September meeting.

"The overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgement, is that what we've done in this monetary medicine is starting to work some," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said, referring to September's interest rate rise.
Figures published after the Fed's announcement showed the US economy growing at a stronger pace than expected, with inflation running above the Fed's target.
An interest rate tells people and businesses how much it costs to borrow money – such as with credit cards, mortgages, or business loans – but also what return they get for saving cash.
The Fed influences interest rates in the US through its target range for the federal funds rate, which is the interest rate used by commercial banks for overnight borrowing.
In its decision to hold rates steady this month, the Fed said that while inflation remains high, it wanted to gather more information before making another decision to change rates.
The Fed also noted that while there was uncertainty, the US economy remained resilient.
Warsh acknowledged that inflation remained too high, but noted that there were other signs - such as tightening credit conditions - that the economy was moving in the right direction.
There is plenty more economic data to come between now and the committee's next meeting, the Fed chair added, which should paint a more detailed picture of the state of the economy.
At that point, Warsh said, "we'll be, I think, better positioned to determine the right policy decision and the stance of policy."
While last month the committee signalled there could be one more rate rise this year, Warsh would not be drawn out on where he thinks they will go in six weeks' time.
"A lot of things can happen, so I'm not going to be able to share with you my musings."
The decision to hold rates steady was not unanimous.
While 10 of the 12 committee members voted to keep rates unchanged, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack voted to increase rates to 4%-4.25%, from its current 3.75%-4%.
The bank's next meeting will be held over 8-9 December.
Warsh said things are moving in the right direction, while the US economy is performing very strongly.
The US economy grew by 3.4% on an annualised basis in the three months to September, stronger than analysts had expected.
That strong growth was driven by an acceleration in investment, and strong consumer spending.

While there was an annualised increase in personal spending of 3.8%, the annualised increase in private investment was a huge 19.4% which analysts say was largely due to investment in artificial intelligence.
Inflation is also above the Fed's target range.
Prices increased by 3.7% in the year to September, driven higher by fuel and energy prices which have surged off the back of the war in Iran.
How does the Fed rate affect mortgages, credit cards, and savings?
The Fed uses interest rate changes to try to keep inflation – the rate at which prices change – at 2% a year and keep the job market stable.
When inflation is too high, the Fed tends to raise interest rates.
This tends to mean higher rates from banks and other lenders, which in turn affects spending and saving decisions.

For example, someone refinancing their mortgage or buying a property for the first time could face higher mortgage rates. It could also mean higher interest rates on credit cards or car loans. However, it means higher interest rates on savings as well.
This encourages people and businesses to save more, spend less money, and make less investments. It also encourages companies to hire less people or slow the pace of pay rises.
All of this tends to reduce demand and slow inflation.
When inflation is low or if the Fed believes the economy needs a boost, it cut rates.
The idea is that this will have the opposite affect, with banks dropping rates leading to more spending and less saving from people and businesses.
Leaving the rates unchanged means rates on things like new mortgages or business loans are also less likely to change. It also means interest rates on cash savings are unlikely to rise.
US interest rates have historically moved around quite a bit.
The last time Fed rates were as high as they have been recently was in the lead up to and during the start of the 2008 global financial crisis.
The Fed then dropped rates to historic lows to encourage spending and job creation during the economic slump and kept them at those lows for several years.
They picked up again ahead of the pandemic before dropping to as low as 0%-0.25% during the pandemic. They then rose to highs of 5.25%-5% from the middle of 2023 to August 2024 as inflation jumped.
They had been falling steadily since then, until rates were raised last month.

title: Dowman to miss three matches after appeal rejected
summary: Arsenal's Max Dowman will miss three matches after an appeal against his sending-off during Tuesday's loss at Fleetwood is rejected.
paragraphs: Dowman to miss three matches after appeal rejected
Arsenal's Max Dowman will miss three matches after an appeal against his sending-off during Tuesday's Carabao Cup loss at Fleetwood was rejected.
The 16-year-old midfielder was shown a straight red card in the 85th minute after reacting to a heavy challenge by Fleetwood's Harrison Neal.
Although Dowman did not fully kick out, his foot did make contact with Neal.
The game finished 1-1 before League Two Fleetwood beat the Premier League champions 5-3 on penalties.
Arsenal appealed Dowman's sending-off on Wednesday.
It was Dowman's second red card this month having also been sent off while representing England's Under-19s.
As Dowman left the field, Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta gave him a scathing look and made what appeared to be an angry comment to the young winger.
Arteta said after the game: "When we prepared the context of the match, we were very clear on the things to respect, the things that emotionally we have to dominate. It was very clear."

Dowman was dismissed for violent conduct, which according to the laws of the game is when a player "uses or attempts to use excessive force or brutality against an opponent when not challenging for the ball... regardless of whether contact is made".
The Gunners were already light on options on the wing as Bukayo Saka, Christos Tzolis and Noni Madueke are currently out injured.
Arteta's side return to Premier League action away to Liverpool on Sunday.

title: Hundreds queue for city's new Lego store
summary: Fans queued for hours ahead of the opening of a new Lego Store in Norwich.
paragraphs: Watch: Hundreds queue for city's new Lego store
Hundreds of people queued for the opening of a new Lego store in Norfolk on Thursday morning.
The shop opened its doors at Chantry Place shopping centre on St Stephen's Street in Norwich at 09:00 GMT. The first person in the queue had been there since 04:00 GMT.
Al, 23, joined the queue at 05:00 GMT and told BBC Radio Norfolk: "We've wanted one here for so long. It's going to pull people from such a large area. I can't believe we haven't had it sooner."
Before the Norwich store opened, the nearest official Lego Store for many Norfolk shoppers was in Stratford, east London.
Follow Norfolk news on BBC Sounds, Facebook, external, Instagram, external and X, external.

title: Ανδρουλάκης κατά Γεωργιάδη: «Πολλά από όσα λέει σήμερα ο Κασιδιάρης, τα λέγατε εσείς κάποτε»
summary: Σε ευθεία αντιπαράθεση με τον Άδωνι Γεωργιάδη ήρθε ο Νίκος Ανδρουλάκης στη Βουλή, με την κόντρα των δύο να εκτείνεται από την απαγόρευση πρόσβασης των ανηλίκων στα social media έως...Περισσότερα...
paragraphs: Ανδρουλάκης κατά Γεωργιάδη: «Πολλά από όσα λέει σήμερα ο Κασιδιάρης, τα λέγατε εσείς κάποτε»

Σε ευθεία αντιπαράθεση με τον Άδωνι Γεωργιάδη ήρθε ο Νίκος Ανδρουλάκης στη Βουλή, με την κόντρα των δύο να εκτείνεται από την απαγόρευση πρόσβασης των ανηλίκων στα social media έως τη συγκέντρωση του Ηλία Κασιδιάρη στη Θεσσαλονίκη και τους κυβερνητικούς χειρισμούς στα εθνικά θέματα.
Ο πρόεδρος του ΠΑΣΟΚ υπεραμύνθηκε της επιλογής του κόμματός του να ψηφίσει «παρών» στο νομοσχέδιο για το age ban, απορρίπτοντας την οριζόντια απαγόρευση για τα παιδιά κάτω των 15 ετών.

«Η Παιδοψυχιατρική Εταιρεία που είπε ότι είναι λάθος η οριζόντια απαγόρευση έχει κόμπλεξ με τον κύριο Μητσοτάκη; Και ο Συνήγορος του Παιδιού; Κανείς δεν έχει κόμπλεξ, αυτό είναι ευθύνη», ανέφερε ο Νίκος Ανδρουλάκης, κατηγορώντας την κυβέρνηση για «φαιδρά πολιτικά παιχνίδια» και «εργαλειοποίηση» του ζητήματος.

Στο ίδιο πλαίσιο, εξαπέλυσε επίθεση στην κυβέρνηση για τη διαχείριση της παραπληροφόρησης, υποστηρίζοντας ότι, ενώ επικαλείται την ανάγκη προστασίας των ανηλίκων από τα fake news, η ίδια τροφοδοτεί ένα περιβάλλον προπαγάνδας και τοξικότητας στο διαδίκτυο.

«Μικρόψυχη αντιπολίτευση» καταλόγισε στον πρόεδρο του ΠΑΣΟΚ ο Άδωνις Γεωργιάδης, κατηγορώντας τον ότι επέλεξε να κινηθεί απέναντι στην κοινή γνώμη, λόγω της πολιτικής αντιπαράθεσης με τον πρωθυπουργό.

«Κάνατε λάθος που είπατε “παρών” στο νομοσχέδιο για τα μέσα κοινωνικής δικτύωσης. Σας το λέω και ως γονέας. Έχει 90% αποδοχή», υποστήριξε, προσθέτοντας ότι το ΠΑΣΟΚ καταψήφισε στην πράξη μια πρωτοβουλία που, κατά τον ίδιο, απολαμβάνει ευρείας αποδοχής από τους γονείς.

Σκληρή ήταν η τοποθέτηση του προέδρου του ΠΑΣΟΚ και για τη συγκέντρωση του Ηλία Κασιδιάρη στη Θεσσαλονίκη, ανήμερα της εθνικής επετείου. Ο Νίκος Ανδρουλάκης χαρακτήρισε την εκδήλωση «αποκρουστική σύναξη μίσους και μισαλλοδοξίας» και επέκρινε την απουσία κυβερνητικής ανακοίνωσης.

«Για το ΠΑΣΟΚ δεν έχουν θέση στη Δημοκρατία τα ναζιστικά κατακάθια», δήλωσε, στρέφοντας στη συνέχεια τα πυρά του και προς τον Άδωνι Γεωργιάδη, με αναφορά στο πολιτικό του παρελθόν. «Φυσικά και για τη ΝΔ δεν έχουν θέση αυτά που λέει ο Κασιδιάρης. Έχουμε μετωπική θέση με αυτές τις ιδέες και αυτό το χώρο», απάντησε ο Υπουργός Υγείας.
Η αντιπαράθεση κορυφώθηκε με την αιχμή του προέδρου του ΠΑΣΟΚ προς τον υπουργό Υγείας για τον Ηλία Κασιδιάρη: «Πολλά από όσα λέει σήμερα ο Κασιδιάρης, τα λέγατε εσείς πριν από μερικά χρόνια».
Ανδρουλάκης για τουρκολιβυκό: «Ξεκάθαρη διπλωματική ήττα»

Η αντιπαράθεση επεκτάθηκε και στην εξωτερική πολιτική, με τον Νίκο Ανδρουλάκη να χαρακτηρίζει «ξεκάθαρη διπλωματική ήττα» τις εξελίξεις γύρω από το τουρκολιβυκό μνημόνιο. Μάλιστα, απαντώντας στις κατηγορίες περί μικροψυχίας της αντιπολίτευσης, διερωτήθηκε εάν στην ίδια κατηγορία εντάσσεται και ο Δημήτρης Καιρίδης, ο οποίος είχε επίσης κάνει λόγο για αποτυχία.

«Ναι, πράγματι είναι μία δυσάρεστη εξέλιξη», απάντησε ο Άδωνις Γεωργιάδης, υποστηρίζοντας ότι η κυβέρνηση έχει εργαστεί για την προώθηση των ελληνικών θέσεων «Είναι η πρώτη φορά που 27 χώρες υποστηρίζουν την ελληνική θέση, όχι την τουρκική», ανέφερε, προσθέτοντας ότι το τουρκολιβυκό μνημόνιο δεν έχει ισχύ και δεν μπορεί να προκαλέσει βλάβη.

title: EU chief lays out vision for new Canada partnership at Montreal summit
summary: Ursula von der Leyen continued to use the term "associate member" for Canada despite some opposition of the bloc's members, including Germany.
paragraphs: EU chief lays out vision for new Canada partnership at Montreal summit

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has laid out her vision for what an "associate membership" status for Canada to the EU would look like as officials gather in Montreal to discuss closer ties.
It is "a partnership that comes close to membership than anything we have done before," she said on Thursday's remarks at the two-day Canada-EU summit.
She added it is a type of relationship that would be open "only to our closest partners outside of Europe who are ready to open a new frontier together."
It includes close alignment on governance and policies, and partnering in research and innovation.
For decades, Canada-EU summits took place without much fanfare - but that's not the case for this year's meeting in the Canadian city.
Thursday and Friday's summit is being closely watched for details on how Canada and the European bloc deepen their ties.
Von der Leyen first proposed "opening the door" to Canada last month for what she called an "associate membership" - a status that does not currently exist.

The overture came after Prime Minister Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg, telling EU lawmakers that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".
Carney and many EU member states welcome closer ties, but not all are on board with what to call this new relationship.
Some, like Germany, are questioning the "associate member" term, fearing that Canada is getting preferential treatment ahead of other nations who also want in.

According to reports by multiple news outlets, Germany and other nations successfully lobbied to remove mention of the title in a draft statement ahead of the summit, opting instead for softer language that references an "ever closer association".
Germany's ambassador to Canada, Matthias Lüttenberg, told CTV News on Tuesday that some member states were "a little surprised" by von der Leyen's announcement last month.
While there is broad support for closer ties, the concept of "associate membership" is something that is not clearly understood as it pertains to Canada, he said.

"Germany has been using the term of associate membership for something completely different, which is the relationship of the EU to Ukraine and potentially Moldova", he said, both of which have been trying to join the bloc for many years.
Despite some opposition, von der Leyen has continued to use the term has not addressed the disagreement over the term.
Later on Thursday, Carney and von der Leyen and business leaders from both Europe and Canada will gather for a business forum.
Canadian officials said they also expect agreements to be hammered out on defence, critical minerals, research and trade over the two days.
Speaking to reporters earlier this week, European officials downplayed the possibility of a major announcement on Canada's new relationship with EU, saying much will be sorted in the coming months.

But both Canadian and EU officials have provided some clues on what the relationship could look like, including closer business ties and allowing more students to study on either side of the Atlantic.

Canada also does not plan on paying a membership fee similar to other EU nations, Canadian officials have said. Instead, it is looking at participating in different EU programmes that would benefit both Canada and member states.
And despite some disagreement about the wording, both have signalled they are fully on board with deepening ties.
"The wording is emblematic of the ambition," said one senior Canadian official who was granted anonymity to speak to reporters at a briefing ahead of the summit.

Polls show the majority of Canadians support forging closer ties to Europe, external, though the Conservative opposition in Canada has criticised the effort as a distraction from other issues, like the high cost of living.
"No one's mortgage or grocery bill will come down," said Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre in a statement, adding that Canada already has a free trade pact with the EU.
- What could EU associate member status mean for Canada?
- Canada welcomes EU proposal to become 'associate member'

Since taking office last year, Prime Minister Carney has pushed Canada closer to Europe as his country continues to deal with an ongoing trade war with the US, its neighbour and largest trading customer.
US President Donald Trump has called the idea of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU "laughable", and has threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act".
Canadian officials stressed on Wednesday that their pivot to Europe is not meant to offend anybody, but rather to build on work that was already underway.
Canada recently signed an agreement that gives its defence companies procurement access to the EU's Security and Defence Partnership programme.
It also signed a landmark energy deal with Germany in May that would see the first-ever long-term shipments of liquified natural gas from Canada to Europe in the coming years.
On Thursday, Canada released its new National Security Strategy, the first in two decades, which underlines supporting security and stability in Europe as a priority.
As for what this new relationship status will be called, Carney has said the "nomenclature" does not matter.
"What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians," he said.

title: Πρόκληση Ερντογάν: «Θα εξουδετερώσουμε όσους μπαίνουν εμπόδιο στους στόχους μας»
summary: Την ειλημμένη απόφασή του να «εξουδετερώσει» όσους μπαίνουν εμπόδιο στην επίτευξη των στόχων της χώρας του, εξέφρασε ο Ρετζέπ Ταγίπ Ερντογάν, λίγες μόλις ώρες μετά την παρέμβαση του Κυριάκου Μητσοτάκη στο Συμβούλιο...Περισσότερα...
paragraphs: Πρόκληση Ερντογάν: «Θα εξουδετερώσουμε όσους μπαίνουν εμπόδιο στους στόχους μας»

Την ειλημμένη απόφασή του να «εξουδετερώσει» όσους μπαίνουν εμπόδιο στην επίτευξη των στόχων της χώρας του, εξέφρασε ο Ρετζέπ Ταγίπ Ερντογάν, λίγες μόλις ώρες μετά την παρέμβαση του Κυριάκου Μητσοτάκη στο Συμβούλιο Ασφαλείας του ΟΗΕ για το τουρκολιβυκό μνημόνιο και τα δικαιώματα της Ελλάδας στις θαλάσσιες ζώνες.

«Είμαστε αποφασισμένοι να εξουδετερώσουμε, με τον ίδιο τρόπο, όσους προσπαθούν να παρεμβληθούν ανάμεσα σε εμάς και στους στόχους μας», ανέφερε ο Τούρκος πρόεδρος, κατά την ομιλία του σε εκδήλωση στην Άγκυρα για την Ημέρα της Δημοκρατίας και τη Σύνοδο Κορυφής του Οργανισμού Τουρκικών Κρατών.
Όπως αναφέρει το CNN Turk, κατά την ίδια ομιλία, ο Ερντογάν έκανε λόγο για τον «Αιώνα των Τούρκων», αναφερόμενος στην πορεία της χώρας του και στους στόχους της για την επόμενη περίοδο.

Ο πρόεδρος της Τουρκίας υποδέχθηκε στην αίθουσα εκθέσεων «Millet», στο Μπεστεπέ, αρχηγούς κρατών και εκπροσώπους χωρών που συμμετέχουν στις εργασίες του Οργανισμού Τουρκικών Κρατών, με αφορμή την 103η επέτειο της ίδρυσης της Τουρκικής Δημοκρατίας.

Μεταξύ αυτών ήταν ο πρόεδρος του Καζακστάν, Κασίμ-Τζομάρτ Τοκάγεφ, ο πρόεδρος της Κιργιζίας, Σαντίρ Τζαπάροφ, ο πρόεδρος του Ουζμπεκιστάν, Σαβκάτ Μιρζιγιόγεφ, καθώς και ο πρόεδρος του Τουρκμενιστάν, Σερντάρ Μπερντιμουχαμέντοφ. Αναφέρθηκε επίσης στον πρόεδρο της Τουρκικής Δημοκρατίας της Βόρειας Κύπρου, Τουφάν Ερχιουρμάν, και στην εκπρόσωπο του Αζερμπαϊτζάν, Τζεϊχούν Μπαϊράμοβα.

Στην ομιλία του, αναφέρθηκε στον Μουσταφά Κεμάλ Ατατούρκ και στους πρωταγωνιστές του εθνικοαπελευθερωτικού αγώνα, τιμώντας τους πεσόντες, τους βετεράνους και τα μέλη της Εθνοσυνέλευσης εκείνης της περιόδου.

«Η Δημοκρατία μας, η οποία ανακηρύχθηκε πριν από 103 χρόνια με το ιδανικό να αποτελεί στήριγμα για όσους δεν έχουν κανέναν, έγινε πηγή ελπίδας τόσο για τον αγαπημένο μας λαό όσο και για τους καταπιεσμένους και αδικημένους λαούς του κόσμου», δήλωσε.
Ο Ερντογάν υποστήριξε ακόμη ότι η Τουρκική Δημοκρατία, με πληθυσμό 86 εκατομμυρίων ανθρώπων, έχει καταγράψει σημαντικά επιτεύγματα σε πολλούς τομείς και συνεχίζει την αναπτυξιακή της πορεία.
Το μήνυμα Μητσοτάκη για το τουρκολιβυκό μνημόνιο

Εξάλλου, λίγο νωρίτερα, ο Κυριάκος Μητσοτάκης είχε αναφερθεί στο τουρκολιβυκό μνημόνιο κατά την παρέμβασή του στο Συμβούλιο Ασφαλείας του ΟΗΕ, επισημαίνοντας ότι η Ελλάδα και η Λιβύη έχουν δικαίωμα να οριοθετήσουν τις θαλάσσιες ζώνες τους βάσει του Διεθνούς Δικαίου.

«Η Ελλάδα και η Λιβύη είναι φυσικοί γείτονες στη θάλασσα, με αντικείμενες ακτές, και έχουν το δικαίωμα, βάσει του Διεθνούς Δικαίου, να οριοθετήσουν τις θαλάσσιες ζώνες τους μέσω συμφωνίας», ανέφερε χαρακτηριστικά ο πρωθυπουργός.
Αντίθετα, υποστήριξε ότι η Τουρκία και η Λιβύη δεν διαθέτουν αντικείμενες ή παρακείμενες ακτές, αλλά επιχείρησαν να καθορίσουν ένα θαλάσσιο σύνορο μεταξύ τους.
«Αυτό είναι παράλογο. Δεν υπάρχει προηγούμενο για μια τέτοια διαγώνια οριοθέτηση», τόνισε.
Ο πρωθυπουργός υπογράμμισε επίσης ότι η συμφωνία Τουρκίας και Λιβύης αγνοεί την παρουσία των ελληνικών νησιών ανάμεσα στις δύο χώρες.

«Η Τουρκία και η Λιβύη έχουν προσπαθήσει να χαράξουν ένα θαλάσσιο σύνορο μεταξύ τους, ωσάν να μην υπάρχουν τα ελληνικά νησιά που βρίσκονται ανάμεσα στις ακτές τους», ανέφερε, προσθέτοντας ότι τα νησιά δεν μπορούν να αντιμετωπίζονται ως ακατοίκητοι βράχοι, καθώς διαθέτουν πληθυσμό, μακρά ιστορία και οικονομική δραστηριότητα.

title: Σέρρες: Ασανσέρ καταστήματος έπεσε τραυματίζοντας δύο γυναίκες
summary: Στο νοσοκομείο τραυματισμένες οδηγήθηκαν δύο γυναίκες μετά από πτώση ασανσέρ σε κατάστημα στην πόλη των Σερρών.Περισσότερα...
paragraphs: Σέρρες: Ασανσέρ καταστήματος έπεσε τραυματίζοντας δύο γυναίκες
Στο νοσοκομείο τραυματισμένες οδηγήθηκαν δύο γυναίκες μετά από πτώση ασανσέρ σε κατάστημα στην πόλη των Σερρών.

Σύμφωνα με τις πληροφορίες του lionnews.gr, ανελκυστήρας ανοιχτού τύπου, που χρησιμοποιείται για τη μεταφορά εμπορευμάτων, έπεσε στο υπόγειο καταστήματος, κάτω από συνθήκες που παραμένουν μέχρι στιγμής αδιευκρίνιστες.
Στο σημείο κινητοποιήθηκαν άμεσα δύο ασθενοφόρα του ΕΚΑΒ και τρία οχήματα της Πυροσβεστικής Υπηρεσίας, προκειμένου να συνδράμουν στην αντιμετώπιση του περιστατικού.
Κατά τις ίδιες πληροφορίες, δεν χρειάστηκε επιχείρηση απεγκλωβισμού, ενώ οι δύο τραυματισμένες γυναίκες διατηρούσαν τις αισθήσεις τους κατά τη μεταφορά τους με τα ασθενοφόρα.
Πρόκειται για την 56χρονη ιδιοκτήτρια της επιχείρησης καθώς και μία 29χρονη.

title: Duckett and Dawson deliver in England's consolation win
summary: Ben Duckett hits 167 and Liam Dawson takes four wickets as England end the tri-series with victory over Sri Lanka.
paragraphs: Duckett and Dawson deliver in England's consolation win
England 386-5 (50 overs): Duckett 167 (132); Asitha 2-63
Sri Lanka 331 (45.1 overs): Rathnayake 118 (77); Dawson 4-49
Ben Duckett's sublime century and four wickets for Liam Dawson earned England a consolation win over Sri Lanka in their final match of the tri-series.

Duckett struck a majestic 167 from 132 balls as England racked up 386-5 in Lahore, which set up a tantalising chase after Sri Lanka's astonishing pursuit of 430 in their previous encounter a week ago.

In another high-scoring match with very little contest between bat and ball, the chase followed a similar trajectory, as Sri Lanka kept themselves within touching distance of the run-rate throughout and needed 87 off the final 10 overs.
But England's bowlers held their nerve on this occasion, closing out a 55-run win as the brilliant Pavan Rathnayake's 118 off just 77 balls was in vain for Sri Lanka.

Rathnayake, who made 130 in last week's carnage, set the platform alongside Kusal Mendis' 89 but Sri Lanka lost their last five wickets for just 16 runs, with Dawson claiming the key scalp of Rathnayake in the 45th over as they were all out for 331.
It meant Duckett's second consecutive century eclipsed Rathnayake's effort, as England's opener capitalised on a batting-friendly surface and a tiring Sri Lanka attack.
The opening partnership between Duckett and Tom Banton impressed again as the pair added 163 together before the latter frustratingly dragged on to his stumps for a fine 74.

Duckett kicked on to his highest ODI score and though England fell short of the 400 mark, contributions of 44 from Harry Brook, 30 from Will Jacks and a quickfire 43 off 27 from Jordan Cox ensured they still posted a commanding total.
Such is the power of England's middle order that Root was not required to bat.
It was far from ideal for Sri Lanka's bowlers to toil in the heat as they face Pakistan in the tri-series final on Sunday, while England travel to Australia for three ODIs and five T20s in November.
While Duckett's 105 against Pakistan held a poor England innings together, here he was ruthless.

With very little swing or seam movement on offer, Duckett was able to back himself to flay anything wide of the off stump and timed the ball exquisitely off his pads when Sri Lanka were forced to bowl straighter.
They attempted to test with the short ball, too, but he was particularly prolific against it as the seamers lacked the pace to really trouble him.

It was also an impressive display of fitness from a player who has spoken about how hard he has worked at that part of his game, eventually falling in the 42nd over from a miscued ramp as the fatigue appeared to take its toll.

Duckett seems to relish opening with Banton: the pair have stands of 143, 6, 91, 74, 4 and 163 in their past six outings together. That, and Banton's form, has given England's selectors an intriguing conundrum for when Jacob Bethell returns from injury in Australia.

Bethell previously occupied the opening slot alongside Duckett but Banton, with five scores of fifty plus in his past six knocks, looks likely to have nailed down his place on this tour, despite some frustration that he could not kick on to three figures when conditions were so favourable.
"You want options, and guys to push their case when they get their opportunities," England coach Brendon McCullum told Sky Sports after the game.
"They're good problems for us to have. We will learn more about that in Australia, but we will always do what's right for the team depending on conditions and the opposition."

Bethell's versatility could potentially see him find a place in the middle order, but it is a promising indication of England's impressive white-ball depth that it is unclear who he could replace from Root, Brook and Jacks, with Jordan Cox needed as keeper in Jos Buttler's injury absence.

The tri-series has exposed some of England's inexperienced bowling, particularly in the middle overs, and with Jamie Overton missing out to Sonny Baker it looked like England were going to rue the omission of leg-spinner Adil Rashid again.

The experienced Dawson saved their blushes though, starting with the crucial wicket of opener Avishka Fernando, who picked out Jacks on the boundary to break a second-wicket stand of 82. Dawson then pinned the explosive Dasun Shanaka lbw for four after Root surprisingly had Mendis caught down the leg side.

Rathnayake raced to a 70-ball century to keep Sri Lanka in contention, and a fifth-wicket stand of 72 off just 38 balls with the explosive Janith Liyanage had England twitching before the latter fell to Baker for 27 off 17.

Dawson then added Rathnayake and Asitha Fernando to his tally when the run-rate spiralled in the closing stages, while Sam Curran and Baker also executed well at the death to recover from their expensive starts early in the innings.

The question surrounding England's second spinner remains, however, as part-timers Jacks and Root conceded 71 off seven combined overs which could have given Brook a headache had Sri Lanka's run chase progressed deeper.
"Leg-spin hasn't played too much of a role and we want to be a team who can adapt to different conditions and be quite malleable with our selections," McCullum added.
"Liam Dawson is an experienced and highly competitive player who's put his hand up here and unfortunately for Rash here, the conditions probably haven't really favoured him."

Sri Lanka 331 (45.1 overs): Rathnayake 118 (77); Dawson 4-49

Ben Duckett's sublime century and four wickets for Liam Dawson earned England a consolation win over Sri Lanka in their final match of the tri-series.

Duckett struck a majestic 167 from 132 balls as England racked up 386-5 in Lahore, which set up a tantalising chase after Sri Lanka's astonishing pursuit of 430 in their previous encounter a week ago.

In another high-scoring match with very little contest between bat and ball, the chase followed a similar trajectory, as Sri Lanka kept themselves within touching distance of the run-rate throughout and needed 87 off the final 10 overs.

But England's bowlers held their nerve on this occasion, closing out a 55-run win as the brilliant Pavan Rathnayake's 118 off just 77 balls was in vain for Sri Lanka.

Rathnayake, who made 130 in last week's carnage, set the platform alongside Kusal Mendis' 89 but Sri Lanka lost their last five wickets for just 16 runs, with Dawson claiming the key scalp of Rathnayake in the 45th over as they were all out for 331.

title: Alaska governor orders probe into Democratic campaign's alleged links to same-name candidate
summary: The Republican governor was responding to allegations in the New York Times that Democrats recruited a spoiler candidate, Dan Sullivan.
paragraphs: Alaska governor orders probe into Democratic campaign's alleged links to same-name candidate
The Republican governor of Alaska has ordered an investigation into an alleged "scheme" which led to two Dan Sullivans standing in the state's US Senate race.

Governor Mike Dunleavy said he was responding to a New York Times (NYT) story, external which said the team of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola worked with people who tried to recruit spoiler candidates in the Senate race.
The governor's post on X said he would investigate "whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws". He did not say which laws he had in mind.
Dan Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator running for re-election, and allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters. Peltola's team deny any wrongdoing.
They say they did not encourage the second Dan Sullivan, a retired teacher who lives in a remote fishing village, to stand. He has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.

The Alaska race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest of the upcoming US midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress. Americans head to the polls across the country on Tuesday.
Dunleavy's statement, which did not name the Peltola campaign, said the NYT reporting had supported findings by the state Division of Elections earlier this year.

"I am therefore directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted," he wrote. "The evidence will determine what happens next."

The NYT report alleged that people connected to Peltola's campaign, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), worked to try to recruit Sullivan the schoolteacher to stand in the Senate race.
This was part of a broader effort to encourage other would-be "spoiler" candidates to enter the race and dilute the support of the sitting Republican senator, the newspaper reported.

The paper said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the NYT's reporting.
The DSCC did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Dunleavy's investigation.
The ballot paper is set to list the two men as Dan S Sullivan, who will be described as the incumbent Republican senator, and Daniel J Sullivan Jr.
Senator Dan Sullivan told Fox News on Wednesday night that Peltola should "come clean" and described it as a scandal of the highest order.
His fellow Republican senator in Alaska, Lisa Murkowksi, accused the Democratic campaign of engaging in a "pattern of lies". President Donald Trump has called for Peltola to be barred.

Previous efforts by the Republicans to remove the non-incumbent Sullivan from the ballot have already been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court which found no state laws had been broken by him running in the race.

Though officials at the state and federal level have called for investigations in the wake of the New York Times reporting, election law experts said it was unlikely to dislodge the second Dan Sullivan from the ballot and it was unclear at this point if any state laws had been violated.

"It turns out that convincing somebody to run for office is not a crime, even if their name happens to be the same as an incumbent," said Justin Levitt, an election law expert at Loyola Law School and a former justice department official.
The non-incumbent Sullivan had a constitutional right to run and have his name on the ballot, added Ruth Greenwood, an election expert at Harvard Law School.

The Trump administration filed a federal lawsuit last week aimed at preventing the certification of the result if the Trump-backed Sullivan loses, arguing that the presence of both of them on the ballot could confuse voters.
Some legal experts expressed scepticism of the merits of the lawsuit, and their chances of success given Alaska's courts had already allowed the second Sullivan to remain on the ballot.
The actual legal arguments the justice department made were a "frivolous theory," Rick Pildes, an election law expert at New York University, told the BBC.
He noted the lawsuit did not cite a specific provision that the government wanted to enforce, merely a general preamble taken from a sweeping US voting law.
Alaska election officials asked a federal court to dismiss the lawsuit "because the complaint has no legal basis".
The justice department has pledged continued action in the wake of the New York Times' reporting.
"They are cheating, let's call it what it is," Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Fox News on Wednesday.

In a series of Truth Social posts, Trump too pointed to the report and made a variety of allegations against Peltola, who he argued should be removed from the ballot. He repeated his endorsement for Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator, writing: "Dan is a GREAT man, has ALWAYS delivered for Alaska."
Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.

The battle threatens to delay the full picture of nationwide results following the midterm elections. The ultimate question of which party controls Congress will have a significant bearing on the remaining two years of Trump's presidency.

A statement from an Alaskans for Mary spokesperson, written prior to Dunleavy's call for an investigation, said: "Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any DC politician will keep her away from that fight.
"The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign."
In a statement given to US media, the DSCC likewise denied that it had been involved in any such scheme.
Peltola earlier this week paused campaigning activities in order to recover after she and her family sustained "minor injuries" in a car crash.

title: Audio reveals exchanges between Spain train operators and drivers moments before deadly crash
summary: The leaked tapes appear to show one high-speed train was given clearance to move at normal speed, even though another up ahead had stalled.
paragraphs: Audio reveals exchanges between Spain train operators and drivers moments before deadly crash

Leaked audio recordings that were published in Spanish media have revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before a deadly crash on Wednesday morning, that has killed 69 people.
Officials are investigating the cause of the disaster, which occurred when a train from Madrid to Seville barrelled into a stationary train.

Three audio recordings between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stalled on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said that authorities will "get to the bottom of every last detail of this tragedy".

Dozens of people were injured, with survivors recounting harrowing scenes people crying and bleeding, passengers trapped in their seats, missing limbs and smoke billowing throughout the carriages, one of which caught fire.
On Thursday, Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia visited some of the injured passengers in a hospital in Toledo.
He later expressed condolences to the victims' relatives, pledging that the investigation would determine why the crash happened, and what measures would be taken for this not to happen again.
The crash is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. On Thursday, the country began three days of national mourning.
The moving train, run by state-owned operator Renfe, had 397 passengers on board. The stationary train was run by private operator Iryo, and carrying 147 passengers.
A reported issue with the automatic signalling system - a computer failure - had forced all trains to halt on the affected stretch.
But later the Renfe train was ordered to proceed in "error", according to Spain's transport minister.
The audio recordings were published by several Spanish news outlets including El Pais and RTVE.
In one, a control centre operator is speaking to the driver of the Renfe train, which was having some technical difficulties.
After some exchanges, the control operator tells the driver: "Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation."
The driver replies: "At normal speed?" To which the controller answers: "Yes."
The Lateral Signalling Block is a back-up or alternative train system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.
The driver of the stationary Iryo train says in another audio recording that communication with the train-control system has been lost, and it is not moving.
The train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda", the driver tells the control centre operator. After a series of exchanges, the driver is then told to "resume the journey" normally.

The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.
The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.
Iryo said its carriages were "struck from behind" by the other train.
Spain's transport minister Óscar Puente said on Wednesday that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".

The leaking of the audio recordings has been criticised by some Spanish politicians, with Alberto Ibáñez, a member of Congress for the left-wing Sumar platform, writing on X that they were "despicable".

Irene Montero - the prime ministerial candidate for the left-wing Podemos party - said responsibility for the crash should not be placed on one worker, adding that train drivers and experts have been warning against the liberalisation of the railway sector for years.

From the crash site, Sánchez said: "We are working day and night not only to support the victims' families, but also to establish every last detail of this tragedy and strengthen safety measures to ensure it never happens again."
Most Spanish politicians have cancelled all public engagements and suspended their campaigning ahead of a snap election on 29 November.

The exception is the far-right party Vox. Its leader, Santiago Abascal, said his party would not take part in what he described as attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of the country's rail infrastructure.

Overnight, around 1,500 people gathered outside the Spanish transport ministry building in the capital, according to broadcaster TVE, which reported that demonstrators were largely calling for the resignations of Sánchez and Puente.
Police used tear gas to disperse crowds after protesters hurled bottles and flares. No injuries or arrests were reported.
Rail drivers went ahead with a planned strike on Thursday, with the Spanish Union of Railway Drivers (Semaf) saying the strike action was being held "in defence of railway safety".
The leader of Spain's main opposition People's Party Alberto Núñez Feijóo said: "Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure."

At the crash site, emergency crews worked through the night under powerful floodlights to cut open metal carriages in the search for victims, with many of those killed in the crash still to be identified.

Hundreds of personnel have been deployed to the disaster site to assist with recovery efforts, Spain's interior ministry said, with drones and helicopters being used to find victims and remove rubble.
A spokesperson for the Spanish Civil Guard told the BBC they had deployed more than 900 people from different specialist departments, and the priority now was identifying the deceased.
They said they did not know how long this would take, but urged those with missing family members to go to one of the local centres which have been set up to offer DNA samples.

title: Faisal Islam: This Budget was micro and that was deliberate
summary: Chancellor John Healey's plans fall short of radical action to create a promised new economic model.
paragraphs: Faisal Islam: This Budget was micro and that was deliberate
It was not a mini Budget, but it was rather small. It might be called the "micro Budget".
Small does not necessarily mean bad, but it clearly falls short of radical action to create a promised new economic model.
A new "theory of growth" was not unveiled as promised by the prime minister Andy Burnham.
It was preamble, roadmap, consultation, perhaps the starter to the main course, which appears to be the PM's 10-year plan next month.
It went unsaid, but the clear stategic aim of Healey's statement was to be the "anti-mini Budget".

This "steady as she goes" predictable fiscal event set out to avoid the aftermath seen following Liz Truss's mini-budget, in which unexpected and unfunded tax cuts spooked the bond and currency markets.

The markets didn't even flicker on Healey's announcement of £65bn of extra borrowing over the next five years - government interest costs have actually fallen since Wednesday, against the backdrop of market turmoil due to the US-Iran war.
The core of the Budget was to get Downing Street through the impacts of the Middle East conflict shock on energy and borrowing costs.
If these pressures prove enduring there are some unpalatable decisions that will have to be grasped within the next year. The can will have to be picked up rather than kicked down the road again.
It buys more time, more "breathing space", as it were, for the government and the prime minister's long-term strategic plans.
The detail may come more quickly than feared. On welfare, the Milburn Review process is clearly heading for some sort of welfare-to-work scheme, even a separate system for younger workers.
It will cost money up front to subsidise work opportunities and hope to save more from welfare bills in the future. The chancellor saw at close quarters Gordon Brown do this twice two decades ago.
The Office for Budget Responsbility's (OBR) economic forecast showed the sheer rise in the welfare bill, which is set to jump to £431bn in 2031, if pensioner support is included.
There are two further areas where the chancellor laid down markers, with little fiscal cost, in terms of the long term plan.
On energy, there is some significance to the "cheaper power" mission announced, reshaping what had previously been a focus on clean power.
While still committed to Net Zero, a series of technical changes to powers over levies and renewable auctions, will seek to turn the tide on additional pressures on energy costs.
On devolution, the plan to allow local mayors to keep some extra business rate and income tax revenues, are more radical than expected.

There are trade offs here, but it essentially provides incentives for regional leaders to grow their economies, workforce and tax base, that are normal elsewhere, but have not existed in the UK's very centralised tax system.
How the PM will square other aspects of his "theory of growth" with the chancellor's spending constraints is the other significant challenge.
Can he announce a 10-year plan without detailing the Liverpool to Manchester high speed train line, or a rebirth of some cancelled HS2 lines he championed a year ago?

Away from the long term, the OBR forecast point to a very tricky economic backdrop until the spring, and a trickier spending review, given the need to accommodate the new defence target of 3% of national income by 2030.
The PM's insistence he will not call an election for a year are eminently believable given the risk of 5% inflation and declining household income.
A "focused" Budget at an uncertain time achieved its narrow aim of a bit of "breathing space" for households and also for the government itself.
But the evident gaps in the Budget will need filling in come the PM's upcoming 10-year plan.

title: Burnham says he wants to cut welfare bill 'as soon as we possibly can'
summary: Opponents have questioned the Budget's lack of detail on welfare reform, with the prime minister not outlining a timetable for any reductions.
paragraphs: Burnham says he wants to cut welfare bill 'as soon as we possibly can'
Andy Burnham has said he wants to cut the welfare bill "as soon as we possibly can", but was unable to guarantee this would happen before the next general election.
Opponents raised concerns over the lack of details on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, after welfare spending was forecast to increase from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2031/32.
Asked whether he would seek to reduce the bill before the next election, Burnham told reporters: "We want to get the welfare bill down as quickly as possible, and we're working flat out to that end."
He warned against "crude cuts" and said he wants to get people into "sustainable employment". The Conservatives accused Labour of being "addicted to welfare".

The prime minister faced questions about his approach after the Treasury disputed that Chancellor John Healey had suggested to the BBC that the benefits bill will be cut before the next election, which must be held by August 2029.

When Healey was asked by the Today Programme on Radio 4 whether there would be a cut in the bill before polling day, he said: "There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way."
But several Treasury sources took issue with this being interpreted as a promise to do so by the next election. Downing Street later said it was "not setting an arbitrary target or timetable".

The prime minister's official spokesman would not say whether the government's ambition to cut welfare spending meant reducing it below its current level, or ensuring that future spending rises at a slower rate than is currently projected.
Further details about the government's proposals are expected after two major reports are published in November.

These include a review of disability benefits co-chaired by Labour minister Sir Stephen Timms and one on young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) led by former minister Alan Milburn.

The two reviews were announced by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer after his attempt to make significant changes to the welfare system, including restricting eligibility for some health-related benefits, resulted in a mass revolt of Labour MPs and an embarrassing climbdown in June 2025.
Speaking during a visit to Derby, Burnham said the "big next priority in front of us" is the publication of the Milburn report.
He said: "We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There's no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible."
Pressed again for a timeline on his plans, the prime minister said: "We're working hard to cut the welfare bill as soon as we possibly can. But we're doing it in a way that supports people into work.
"If we just went and made crude cuts, in the end, that leaves people in crisis, and you spend more public money somewhere else, so it's about getting people into sustainable employment."

Former Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane said if the government could provide a plan to show "greater restraint" of the benefits bill, that would "play spectacularly well" with the financial markets.
Haldane, who has previously advised Burnham, told the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast: "If the government could get that through I think it would come with a huge bonus."
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch responded to the Budget by saying the country was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed, and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".
Reacting to government briefings and remarks on Thursday related to when a reduction in the benefits bill could take place, Badenoch said it "looks like foot in mouth syndrome is spreading".
She said: "Don't let anyone tell you this was a 'do no harm budget'. In doing so little, Labour have harmed our economic security and they've harmed our national security."
Welfare spending is forecast to rise this year by £19bn to £353bn.
Watchdog and forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said this figure is expected to rise to £431bn in 2031/32, driven primarily by health-related and pensioner benefit spending.

Of the figure forecast for 2031/32, £209.8bn is on pensioners, including the state pension and winter fuel payments, while £110.7bn is on universal credit and legacy equivalents and £69.6bn is on disability benefits such as personal independence payments.
The government has already pledged to reform the existing state pension triple lock from 2030, and more proposals and changes to the welfare system are expected to emerge in the coming months.

The prime minister faced questions about his approach after the Treasury disputed that Chancellor John Healey had suggested to the BBC that the benefits bill will be cut before the next election, which must be held by August 2029.

When Healey was asked by the Today Programme on Radio 4 whether there would be a cut in the bill before polling day, he said: "There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way."

But several Treasury sources took issue with this being interpreted as a promise to do so by the next election. Downing Street later said it was "not setting an arbitrary target or timetable".

title: Patrick Stewart, ‘Star Trek’ Captain and ‘X-Men’ Superhero, Dies at 86
paragraphs: Patrick Stewart, the sophisticated actor who brought a Shakespearean touch to Star Trek and X-Men as he made an otherworldly transformation from British stage veteran to sci-fi icon, has died. He was 86.
Stewart died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles following “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia,” longtime spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak announced.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”
In the late 1980s, Stewart had decades of classical theater work in England under his belt but was unfamiliar in America when he was given command of the U.S.S. Enterprise.

Star Trek: The Next Generation producer Robert Justman happened upon a UCLA lecture featuring Stewart and witnessed him reading from Shakespeare in his trademark patrician style. Justman called the actor in for an audition against the wishes of Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry, who didn’t think a bald Brit could be the face of the new series.

After a contentious casting process, Stewart won over the famously persnickety Roddenberry and signed a long-term contract to play Capt. Jean-Luc Picard, thinking there was no way the show would last beyond one season.

“Every single person I spoke to — agents, directors, screenwriters, other actors — said, ‘Oh, don’t worry about six years. You’ll be lucky to make it through the first year,’ ” Stewart recalled in 2010. “Everybody felt it was madness to try to revive an iconic series like William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy‘s Star Trek. So, on the basis of that advice, I signed the six-year contract.”

The Los Angeles Times referred to him as an “unknown British Shakespearean actor” in a story announcing his casting. Brent Spiner, who played the android Data on the show, fashioned a sign to go above Stewart’s dressing room that read in bright red, “WARNING: Unknown British Shakespearean Actor.”

Next Generation premiered in September 1987, two months after Stewart’s 47th birthday, and initially struggled to catch on with Star Trek fans, many of whom considered the new cast to be pretenders to the throne. But after ups and downs, the series soared to new heights in 1990 with the season-three finale, “Best of Both Worlds.”

That episode featured the first cliffhanger in Star Trek history and saw Picard abducted and assimilated by an alien race known as The Borg. It was a genuinely shocking moment pulled off decades before such twists became common on the small screen.

Stewart also was at the center of several episodes considered among history’s finest hours of sci-fi television, including the alternate timeline-focused “Yesterday’s Enterprise” in 1990 and 1992’s “The Inner Light,” which had Picard live an entire lifetime, all in the blink of an eye.

Stewart and his cast of Americans became known as one of the closest in television, but in the early years, the theater veteran had trouble accepting the jokes that accompanied a typical 14-hour day on the set.
“Those guys taught me that you can do good work and have a good time at the same time,” he said in 2013. “Before that, I had always thought the two were unconnected completely.”

Next Generation ended in 1994 after seven seasons, going out with an Emmy nomination for outstanding drama series and spawning four films: Star Trek: Generations (1994), co-starring Shatner; Star Trek: First Contact (1996); Star Trek: Insurrection (1998); and Star Trek: Nemesis (2002), which saw Stewart face off against a then-unknown Tom Hardy as a younger clone of Picard.

Stewart acknowledged that Star Trek saw him fall victim to typecasting, so when he was offered the role of Prof. Charles Xavier in X-Men (2000) in the final years of Next Generation‘s movie run, he was hesitant.

An adaptation of the Marvel comic books, X-Men was a pioneering film and helped launch a new age of superhero cinema. Stewart worked opposite longtime friend Ian McKellen, who played the villain Magneto, and appeared as Xavier in seven more films, starring in X2: X-Men United (2003), X-Men: The Last Stand (2006), X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014) and Logan (2017) and having cameos in X-Men Origins: Wolverine (2009), The Wolverine (2013) and Avengers: Doomsday (2026).
Portraying Picard and Xavier for many years allowed him to explore layers upon layers with his characters, an opportunity few actors ever get.

“Both of them … I immensely admired for their morality, for their kindness, for their sensitivity, for their compassion,” Stewart told THR‘s Stephen Galloway in 2017. “Even for their intellectual capacities. Playing Jean-Luc for all those years had a real impact on me.”
After 17 years away, he returned to a familiar world to star in the CBS All Access series Star Trek: Picard, which debuted in January 2020.

Stewart was born on July 13, 1940, in Mirfield, Yorkshire, England, to Alfred and Gladys Stewart. His father worked as a semi-skilled laborer and was a veteran of World War II, among the last men evacuated from Dunkirk.

A heavy drinker, Alfred was physically abusive toward his wife, but not his three sons. It was only decades later that Stewart learned his dad’s violent behavior likely stemmed from undiagnosed post-traumatic stress disorder.

The youngest in the family, Stewart found himself terrified at home and often tasked with getting between his father’s fists and his mother. Growing up under those circumstances led him to advocate for veterans as well as domestic abuse victims later in life.

“I managed to find my own refuge in acting. The stage was a far safer place for me than anything I had to live through at home — it offered escape. I could be someone else, in another place, in another time,” he wrote in 2009.

At 15, he got a job at the local newspaper, The Dewsbury Reporter, where he was tasked with interviewing bereaved family members when someone would die in the town. Journalism turned out not to be his passion, and he spent much of his free time with drama groups. His editor finally told him he had to choose between acting and journalism — and he quit on the spot.

To support himself, Stewart got a sales job at a furniture store, but by 18 he had won a scholarship to Bristol Old Vic Theatre School. At 26, he became a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, spending much of the 1960s with the group as well as with the National Theatre.

After a series of roles in British film and television, he made his U.S. debut in John Boorman’s King Arthur film Excalibur (1981), then appeared as the minstrel Gurney Halleck in David Lynch‘s cult sci-fi classic Dune (1984).
Stewart received Emmy and Golden Globe nominations for playing Captain Ahab in the 1998 miniseries Moby Dick and for his work as King Henry II in 2003’s The Lion in Winter.

A humorous guest spot on the HBO comedy Extras, in which he portrayed a lecherous version of himself obsessed with seeing women naked, earned him another Emmy nom in 2006, and he was nominated yet again in 2010, for playing King Claudius in the Royal Shakespeare Company’s Hamlet.

In 2015-16, he starred as cantankerous British talk show host Walter Blunt on Starz’s Blunt Talk, which earned him a third Golden Globe nom. He also had a long-running gig as the voice of Avery Bullock on American Dad!
He portrayed Bosley in Elizabeth Banks’ reboot of Charlie’s Angels (2019) and this year had a voice role in The Sheep Detectives.

On the 2001 New Year Honours list, Queen Elizabeth II appointed him an Officer of the Order of the British Empire, and he was knighted by her in 2010. “I never imagined anything like that could possibly happen to me, and in fact, it is still a significant unreality to me,” he said.

Stewart was married three times. He wed theater choreographer Sheila Falconer in 1966, and the pair remained together until 1990. They had two children, Daniel — who appeared in Blunt Talk — and Sophia. He was married to Star Trek producer Wendy Neuss from 2000-03 before wedding jazz musician Sunny Ozell in a 2013 ceremony officiated by McKellen.

“Like me, Jean-Luc has lived an unusual life that has taken him far beyond the bounds of normal human experience,” he wrote in his 2023 memoir, Making It So. “But he is also someone who has remained true to his earthbound roots, for they are what gave him his identity. In the end, he feels the call of home, as do I.”

title: Cannes Chief Thierry Fremaux Hails French Film Model as Cnc Head Gaëtan Bruel Vows to Fight for Its Future at 80th Anniversary
summary: France’s National Film Board, the Cnc, marked its 80th anniversary with a three-day gathering of industry leaders in Paris, including Cannes Film Festival chief Thierry Frémaux who praised the country’s unique film funding system. Cnc president Gaëtan Bruel, meanwhile, warned against attempts to dismantle a model that has helped make France a global cinema powerhouse.
paragraphs: France’s National Film Board, the CNC, marked its 80th anniversary with a three-day gathering of industry leaders in Paris, including Cannes Film Festival chief Thierry Frémaux who praised the country’s unique film funding system. CNC president Gaëtan Bruel, meanwhile, warned against attempts to dismantle a model that has helped make France a global cinema powerhouse.

The anniversary celebrations, held from Oct. 26-28 at the Cinémathèque française, came at a particularly fraught moment for the institution which faces growing political scrutiny and budgetary pressures as France heads toward the 2027 presidential election.
Frémaux, who also heads the Institut Lumière in Lyon, highlighted the CNC’s key role on display across films showcased at Cannes and other major festivals.

“We don’t say it because the Americans accuse us of constantly favoring certain things, because they themselves cannot imagine that the selection process is conducted in complete independence. But you can see just how much French money, the CNC and French professionals are absolutely everywhere,” Frémaux said during an onstage conversation with film historian Antoine de Baecque at the French Cinémathèque on Wednesday.
Frémaux also pointed out the CNC’s support for film restoration, noting that countries around the world have begun developing similar initiatives.

“Every country in the world has its masterpieces. And not all masterpieces have been restored, so there is still plenty of work to be done. Many countries are now giving themselves the means to do this, following the French model,” he said.
Frémaux emphasized that France’s film funding system not only supports contemporary production but also helps preserve cinema’s history and nurture future generations of film lovers.

“People are finally beginning to understand that money from cinema goes back into cinema. It has taken a long time, but I’m starting to read things about it. Journalists are always a little slow,” he joked. “But the fact remains that this money from cinema also goes toward cinema’s history. And that brings us back to the fundamental role of building an educational and intellectual foundation for cinephilia as a driving force in protecting contemporary creation.”

The event wrapped with a forceful defense of the institution from Bruel, who took over as CNC president last year and is facing pressures from populist parties, including the far right party Rassemblement National. In its latest budget proposal, unveiled earlier this month, the party outlined plans to strip down the National Film Board, privatize public broadcasting and slash public broadcasting funding

“We are going through, on a global scale, one of the deepest crises this sector has experienced since the invention of cinema,” Bruel said. “These 80 years have not been a smooth ride. They have been marked by successive upheavals. But what we are experiencing today is as though we were facing the ocean head-on, as though the upheavals of eight decades were happening all at once.”
Bruel also pointed to the industry’s shifting power dynamics, as streaming platforms are now facing new competition from YouTube.

“A few years ago, streamers seemed to be triumphing over television and movie theaters. Today, faced with YouTube, they themselves are discovering their vulnerabilities, and they are seeking to converge with traditional broadcasters, a sign that yesterday’s world has not said its last word,” he said.
For Bruel, these changes make the CNC’s mission more important than ever, particularly as public support for the arts faces increasing criticism.

“According to some, the CNC is a dispensable appendage, and all we would need to do is cut it off to get better. You can always cut off an arm, but you’d better be sure of what you stand to gain and what you stand to lose,” he said.

Bruel argued that France’s film funding model also serves a civic role, in giving people access to culture, through an extensive network of movie theaters, as well as film education programs allowing an estimated two million schoolchildren to visit movie theater each year.

The CNC’s 80th anniversary brought together a broad cross-section of France’s film and television industries for three days of discussions exploring the institution’s history and its evolving role in the entertainment landscape.

Among the prominent filmmakers participating were Olivier Assayas, Arnaud Desplechin, Amélie Bonnin and Rachid Hami, alongside producers Anne-Dominique Toussaint, Alex Berger and Simone Harari Baulieu, and leading animation executives including Illumination Studios Paris co-founder Jacques Bled and Xilam Animation founder Marc du Pontavice.

The program explored the defense of theatrical exhibition, the rise of French animation, the expansion of the CNC’s remit into television, video games and immersive creation, and the challenges posed by Hollywood’s global dominance. A panel devoted to protecting movie theaters featured Desplechin alongside exhibitors Aurélie Delage and Camille Labé, and former UGC chief Alain Sussfeld. Another discussion examined the CNC’s expansion into television, bringing together Berger, Harari Baulieu, former CNC director general and Arte president Jérôme Clément, and screenwriter-director Clémence Madeleine-Perdrillat.

Looking ahead, Bruel signaled that the CNC would soon present a broader strategy for digital creators and social media platforms like YouTube, arguing that they should contribute more fairly to the financing of French audiovisual creation, on par with streaming services.

His words on investment alluded to the European Commission’s current review of the Audiovisual Media Service Directive which allows members states to require streaming platforms such as Netflix, Disney+ and Prime Video to invest in European film and television production. The review could also open the door to bringing YouTube under similar investment obligations to level the playing field between broadcasters, streamers and digital platforms.

“Will we remain one in the future? No battle is lost in advance, especially when we have so many strengths in our hands, and you can count on the CNC to play its full part. But the answer, by definition, remains open,” Bruel concluded.

title: Roman Coppola Named Creative Consultant for the 2027 Indie Spirit Awards
summary: Film Independent has appointed Roman Coppola as Creative Consultant for the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards. The organization made the announcement on Thursday. As previously announced, the annual celebration of independent movies and TV will take place Saturday, March 6, 2027 at the Hollywood Palladium.
paragraphs: Film Independent has appointed Roman Coppola as Creative Consultant for the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards. The organization made the announcement on Thursday. As previously announced, the annual celebration of independent movies and TV will take place Saturday, March 6, 2027 at the Hollywood Palladium.

“The Spirit Awards have always celebrated artists who challenge conventions and find new ways to tell stories,” Juan Devis, president of Film Independent, said in a statement. “We believe the Spirits themselves should embrace that same creative freedom. Roman brings a unique sensibility, a sense of play, and a willingness to experiment. We’re excited to work with him to rethink not just the ceremony, but the entire experience of bringing our independent film community together.”
In the newly created role, Coppola will work with the show’s production team to “help shape the tone, visual identity and overall experience of the 2027 Spirit Awards,” according to the organization.

The son of Francis Ford and Eleanor Coppola and brother of Sofia Coppola, Roman has been working in the film industry for nearly his entire life, beginning with his first-ever credit, as an actor, in his father’s 1966 feature, “You’re A Big Boy Now,” when he was a baby. He is a frequent collaborator of Wes Anderson, producing and/or co-writing “The Darjeeling Limited,” “Isle of Dogs,” “The Phoenician Scheme” and other titles. He has collaborated with his sister several times, with producing credits that include “Somewhere” and “The Bling Ring.” He also works in music videos and commercials. In 2013, he was nominated for the Best Original Screenplay Oscar with Anderson for “Moonrise Kingdom.”

“The endless inventiveness of cinema and the unique, diverse ways filmmakers find to express themselves are things I care deeply about,” Coppola said, also via statement. “I’m looking forward to collaborating with the team to create a celebration that’s playful, adventurous, and full of surprises—one that will spotlight the remarkable voices that make independent cinema so vital.”
Nominees for the 2027 Spirit Awards will be announced Dec. 2.

title: BAFTA Trustees Accused of Potentially Violating Charity Law Over Free Ceremony Tickets
summary: BAFTA trustees may have violated U.K. charity and company laws by accepting complimentary awards show tickets that were not disclosed in the organization’s financial accounts, according to allegations raised at the British Academy’s annual general meeting this week.
paragraphs: BAFTA trustees may have violated U.K. charity and company laws by accepting complimentary awards show tickets that were not disclosed in the organization’s financial accounts, according to allegations raised at the British Academy’s annual general meeting this week.

Michael Pritchett, chair of BAFTA’s membership council, said legal advice he commissioned suggested that trustees who approved the organization’s accounts may have committed offenses under the Charities Act and Companies Act, The Guardian reported Wednesday.

The British Academy of Film and Television Arts, which operates as a registered charity, previously allowed trustees to bring guests to its ceremonies, a practice that is said to have been in place for as long as two decades. The complimentary seats reportedly included premium tickets to the BAFTA Film Awards valued at up to £2,000 ($2,660).

Pritchett raised the concerns at BAFTA’s annual general meeting on Monday, arguing that the ticket arrangements conflicted with the organization’s governing rules, which prohibit trustees from receiving remuneration or other benefits from the charity.

The allegations also raise questions about BAFTA’s financial disclosures. The organization’s 2024 and 2025 accounts stated that trustees received no remuneration for their services, while its public register reported no payments or benefits.

According to Pritchett, the legal advice suggested that trustees who approved those accounts may have violated their obligations under U.K. law. He also questioned whether the complimentary tickets should have been subject to taxes dating back to 2016, potentially leaving BAFTA liable for unpaid National Insurance contributions.

Pritchett called for trustees to repay any money owed, settle outstanding taxes and correct the organization’s financial accounts if necessary. He also criticized a senior BAFTA executive for declining to provide records identifying which trustees had received a complimentary ticket.

BAFTA discontinued its longstanding guest-ticket policy in 2025 following a recommendation from its governance committee. The organization has since launched an independent review into the long-running arrangement.

BAFTA’s outgoing chair, Sara Putt, said the organization had already taken the steps to address the concerns and noted that Pritchett’s legal advice was based on limited information, while BAFTA’s own legal advisers had access to a more complete account of the circumstances.

“Trustees of BAFTA are invited to attend events in a working capacity, representing the Academy in an ambassadorial role, and prior to 2025 they could also bring a ‘plus one’ guest to accompany them,” a BAFTA spokesperson told Variety. “In 2025 BAFTA decided to review its guest tickets arrangements and discontinued the long-standing custom and practice of trustees inviting a plus one. The Board has since established an independent review group to consider the historic guest ticket arrangement – the review is underway.”
No legal violations have been formally established.

title: Darren Aronofsky to Receive Director’s Award at Poland’s Camerimage Film Festival
summary: Darren Aronofsky will receive the Award for Director at the 34th ToruńCamerimage International Film Festival in Poland.
paragraphs: Darren Aronofsky will receive the Award for Director at the 34th ToruńCamerimage International Film Festival in Poland.

The festival, which celebrates the art of cinematography, will take place Nov. 7-14 in Toruń, Poland. Organizers announced the honor Thursday, recognizing the Oscar-winning director’s distinctive approach to filmmaking and his longstanding collaborations with cinematographers, particularly Matthew Libatique, who has shot much of the director’s work.

“Honouring Aronofsky at ToruńCamerimage is a tribute to a director whose work demonstrates the immense power of cinema when form becomes an integral part of the story being told,” festival organizers said in a statement.

Aronofsky made his feature directorial debut with the psychological thriller “Pi” in 1998, which earned him the directing award at Sundance. He followed it with 2000’s “Requiem for a Dream,” starring Jared Leto, Jennifer Connelly, Marlon Wayans and Ellen Burstyn, who received an Oscar nomination for her performance.

His 2008 drama “The Wrestler,” starring Mickey Rourke, won the Golden Lion at the Venice Film Festival, while 2010’s “Black Swan,” starring Natalie Portman, earned five Academy Award nominations, including best picture and best director. Portman won the Oscar for best actress for her performance.

Aronofsky’s other directing credits include “The Fountain,” “Noah” and “mother!” His 2022 drama “The Whale” marked Brendan Fraser’s return to a leading film role and earned the actor his first Academy Award. Most recently, Aronofsky directed the 2025 crime thriller “Caught Stealing,” starring Austin Butler, Zoë Kravitz and Regina King.

Camerimage, one of the world’s leading festivals dedicated to cinematography, annually recognizes filmmakers and cinematographers for their contributions to visual storytelling. Its main competition awards the Golden Frog for outstanding cinematography, alongside a series of honorary awards recognizing achievements across the filmmaking industry.
