title: What the Budget means for your money
summary: Changes announced by Chancellor John Healey in his first Budget will affect your finances directly. Here's how.
paragraphs: Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you
Families facing cost-of-living pressures are being offered some help, or "breathing space" as Chancellor John Healey is calling it.
The help comes as prices are rising faster than expected with annual energy bills in particular likely to increase by hundreds of pounds in January.
Here's how the key announcements in the Budget affect you and your money.
If you are living in a home in council tax bands A to D in England, you will receive a one-off £100 "Household Energy Payment" from January, funded by extra tax on banks.
It will be paid directly into your bank account.

Council tax bands are listed below - you can check which one you are in by looking at your annual bill or checking the government's website, external, although that was struggling to cope with traffic after the announcement.
Administrations in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will receive the equivalent funding, and they will decide whether to introduce the same payment.

This is designed to help with soaring energy bills, with some forecasts suggesting a typical annual bill could rise by £400 or so to £2,100 in January the saving will be only a portion of that. Although it's designated for energy bills, you can spend the money on anything you wish.
The VAT cut on electricity bills, which was introduced in October, will also be extended to July. It was due to end in April.
The fee for connecting to your gas supply so called standing charges will be scrapped in England, Scotland and Wales, next year "or as soon as possible after", the chancellor said.
These fixed daily charges will then be shifted onto the price you pay for each unit of energy.
The Treasury calculates that 60% of households will save an average of £45 a year, with lower users gaining the most. But the saving will come after the projected big rise in bills in January.
Higher users - in the biggest houses but also large, low-income families - will pay more than they currently do.
The government wants to extend reforms to electricity standing charges later.
The 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel, introduced by Rishi Sunak in 2022, will be extended to July. It was scheduled to be phased out from January.
It means drivers will still pay the levy at 52.95p per litre.
Motor fuel prices have risen sharply owing to the continued impact of the Iran war on drivers, with diesel having recently hit new records when it moved above £2 per litre.
The cost of filling a typical family car with diesel has gone up by around £30 since late February. A tankful of petrol costs about £23 more.
The chancellor has scrapped his predecessor's plans to reduce the annual amount people can save tax-free in cash in Individual Savings Accounts (Isas).
Rachel Reeves had wanted the policy to encourage personal investment in stocks and shares.
It meant, from April 2027, if you're under 65, you would only be able to save £12,000 a year in cash in an Isa, rather than £20,000.
Instead, the government plans to create a new "Starter Isa" for first-time investors.
If you have a large amount in savings, or if you fail to use the tax-free Isa allowance, then you will pay more tax from April.

You do not pay tax on all savings. There is the annual £20,000 Isa allowance, and an annual savings income allowance (in other words, the interest received on a savings pot) of £1,000 for basic rate taxpayers and £500 for higher-rate taxpayers.
But beyond that savings tax rates will rise by four percentage points to 24% and 44% respectively from April.

Landlords could also pay more in tax. In analysis published on Wednesday, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said these steps along with measures over the past decade that have reduced private landlord returns "collectively risk leading to a steady rise in rents".
Minimum wage rates will rise by 3.9% in April. It means:
- Eligible workers aged 21 and over on the National Living Wage will receive £13.21 an hour, up from £12.71
- If you are aged 18, 19 or 20, the National Minimum Wage will increase to £11.27 an hour, up from £10.85
- For those aged 16 or 17, the minimum wage will rise to £8.31 an hour, up from £8
- The separate apprentice rate which applies to eligible people under 19 - or those over 19 in the first year of an apprenticeship – will also increase to £8.31 an hour, from £8
However, these figures mean, this time around, there's no progress on Labour's manifesto promise to narrow the gap in minimum wages between older and younger workers.
For all workers, the ongoing freeze in the income bands, or thresholds, at which income tax is paid went unmentioned in the Budget.
But it means any kind of pay rise could drag you into a higher tax bracket, or see a greater proportion of your income taxed than would otherwise be expected. Scotland has its own income tax bands.
The triple lock policy means that the state pension will go up in line with average wage increases, at 3.9%.
- the flat-rate state pension for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 will be £250.70 a week, or £13,036.40 a year, up £488 on now
- the old basic state pension for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 will be £192.10 a week, or £9,989.20 a year, up £374.40 on now
The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension.

The chancellor said this would be the case until at least 2030, as there will be a new Pension Tax Allowance, so pensioners with an income up to the value of the full new state pension will not pay income tax.
The First Time Buyer Isa has been in the planning stages with the government for a while.
Healey has confirmed that it is intended to replace the often-criticised Lifetime Isa.
The penalty for withdrawing savings from a Lifetime Isa if you are buying a home above the £450,000 threshold will be scrapped.

Separately, he confirmed the Your First Home equity scheme to allow first-time buyers in England to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.
The government has made no changes to student loan rates - saying only that it is being "kept under review".
There has been some backlash after the previous chancellor froze the repayment threshold for Plan 2 student loans, which were given out for just over a decade in England from 2012.

It means the salary at which borrowers start paying back their loans is due to stay at £29,385 in April and remain there for three years – so graduates start repaying sooner and repay more each month than they would otherwise have done.
The chancellor is tripling the allowance for extra earnings made alongside your main income.

If you sell on Vinted, offer dogwalking, earn money as an influencer, or have any other kind of small-scale side hustle, you can currently earn up to £1,000 a year before you have to report it to HMRC.
From April 2027 that allowance will rise to £3,000.
Some announcements affecting your finances have already been made by the government.

- Tariffs removed from 100 food items such as baked beans and garlic, which the government calculates could save households up to £21 per year - or 40p a week - when combined with existing tariff suspensions that were introduced in June
- Allowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism instead. However, this will not come in until 2030
- Giving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to £194 a week for the period
- Making permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above that

- The prime minister's plan to reinstate the £2 cap on bus fares in England from January to be in effect throughout 2027. Some cities already have caps, and funding is being given to the devolved nations

title: DoorDash to buy Instacart in $17bn deal it says will expand customer options
summary: Instacart shoppers will be able to buy from 150,000 stores, compared to the 100,000 currently available on the platform, the firms said.
paragraphs: DoorDash to buy Instacart in $17bn deal it says will expand customer options
DoorDash will acquire grocery delivery firm Instacart in a $17bn (£12.8bn) deal, creating a behemoth that will bring more meals, quick-need purchases and big weekly shops directly to customers.
DoorDash said the deal, expected to be final in about a year, will expand options for customers and let more sellers use the companies' services.
Instacart shoppers will be able to buy from 150,000 stores, up from the current 100,000, while DoorDash will reach beyond restaurants into retail, the firms said.
"Together, we can accelerate innovation across the grocery industry and make online grocery more seamless and affordable for the millions of households we serve," Instacart's chief executive said.

"Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more," CEO Chris Rogers also said.
For DoorDash, the acquisition will allow it to use Instacart's grocery selection and substitution expertise, the company's co-founder and chief executive, Tony Xu, said.
"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you'd choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts," Xu said.
He added that "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day".
The deal, expected to be done by the end of 2027 or first six months of 2028, is DoorDash's biggest acquisition to date, and could help it take on delivery giants like Amazon.
Morningstar analyst Martin Szumski told Reuters that the growth area in food delivery was shifting.
"Restaurant delivery is maturing, and growth now lies in more frequent, higher-value orders: weekly grocery shops, convenience items, and retail," he said.

In the agreement, DoorDash will acquire Instacart for a value of $65 a share, which would be a 26% premium on the closing price of Instacart stock on 22 October - the price before news of the potential merger first emerged. The deal will be at least 75% cash, DoorDash said.
DoorDash plans to keep Instacart's brand, app, and technology products. The delivery services will keep operating as independent companies until the deal is concluded.
The merger may raise antitrust issues with government regulators, Reuters also reported.

New York City's commission on consumer and worker protections, which last month reached a $131.5m settlement with DoorDash over allegations of underpaying workers, said in a statement: "This proposed merger continues a troubling trend of mega-corporations consolidating."
"Whether or not this merger proceeds, we will fully enforce delivery workers' rights," it added.

title: What we know so far about deadly Spain train crash
summary: More than 500 passengers were on board the trains when the crash occurred in the province of Toledo, south of Madrid.
paragraphs: What we know so far about deadly Spain train crash
Two trains crashed south of the Spanish capital Madrid on Wednesday morning, on the high-speed line to Seville.
At least 69 people died in the collision, when a state-operated Renfe train went into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda.
The crash happened at 08:53 (07:53 GMT) between municipalities Mora and Orgaz, and about 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid, according to an account given by the Spanish government.

The privately run Iryo train appears to have been stationary on the state-run Renfe train barrelled into the back of it at high speed. Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by a Renfe train "due to causes that are still unknown".
The crash caused some carriages to fall down an embankment.
All train traffic on the line was stopped at stations along the route.
Renfe said services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia were suspended.
A passenger on board one of the trains told local media there was a heavy impact about 40 minutes into the journey.
Transport minister Óscar Puente said a computer failure at about 08:30 on Wednesday morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
"In the event of a system failure, the control centre takes over," he said, adding it was the control centre that decided to allow the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.
That decision, Puente said, was made "under inexplicable circumstances". It resulted in the Renfe train crashing into the Iryo train, which was stationary on the tracks some distance ahead.

Audio recordings obtained by Spanish media between train controllers working in Madrid for a rail infrastructure company in Adif in Madrid and the train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move at 08:36 even though another some 25km ahead had stalled.
In one recording, the controller tells the driver of the Renfe train to disconnect and reconnect the LZB mechanism that monitors train speeds, and then resume the journey at normal speed.
"Disconnect and reconnect LZB. Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation," the control centre operator says to the driver.
The driver replies, "At normal speed?" To which the controller says: "Yes."

Under normal protocols, the driver would be expected to continue moving at a maximum of 40km/h according to their line of sight, and not at normal speed on a track designed for speeds of up to 200km/h.
The Lateral Signaling Block is a back-up or alternative train system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.

In a second audio recording between the driver of the Iryo train in front and the control centre, the driver says the train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda". After some exchanges, the control centre operator tells the driver to "resume the journey" normally.

The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.
The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.
- Bloodied, dazed and angry - how passengers' rail journey turned to disaster in Spain
- High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain
More than 540 people were on board both trains.

Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the government of Castilla-La Mancha region, told TVE that one of the trains - managed by the Iryo company - was carrying 146 passengers plus one baby, while the Renfe-managed train had 397 passengers on board.
A former government minister was also among those reported missing.
The Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations (CEOE) posted on X that, Fátima Báñez - who heads the organization's foundation - was on board one of the trains involved in the crash.
More than 100 people were treated for injuries, according to Spanish authorities, and by the next day 50 of them were still in hospital, 15 in a critical condition.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said "the whole of Spain is grieving" and that "lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart".
"The pain is immense," he said on a visit to the crash site.
The government was "trying to determine what was the origin of this tragedy, of this terrible accident," he added.
"We will get to the bottom of this, and if there has been any negligence, it will come to light.
"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."

Opposition conservative leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, whose People's Party leads most opinion polls ahead of 29 November elections, said it was not the day to talk about political responsibility, but insisted "Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure".
Most Spanish politicians cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday and suspended their election campaign.
However, Santiago Abascal of the far-right Vox refused to take part in what his party described as attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of the country's rail infrastructure.
Three days of official mourning began on Thursday.
Spain's royal family posted on X that it was "shocked and concerned" and expressed condolences for the relatives of the deceased and those affected by the crash.
A spokesperson for the EU said the bloc was ready to help Spain if needed.
A huge emergency response was under way with fire crews and helicopters at the scene.
Hospitals in the area suspended planned surgeries as they deal with an influx of patients from the crash, Spanish media have reported.
A blood transfusion centre in Madrid appealed for "urgent" donations. In a post on X, Centro de Transfusión said it made the request "in the face of a possible sudden increase in care needs".
It reported that facilities in Toledo, Ciudad Real and Alcázar de San Juan had cancelled procedures as casualties from the crash begin to arrive.
The Spanish Civil Guard set up bureaus in Madrid, Toledo, Seville and Córdoba to investigate reports of missing persons.
"The top priority is the identification of the missing persons and the taking of DNA samples to be able to locate their relatives," the civil guard wrote in a post on X.
This is the second high-speed rail tragedy in Spain this year.
In January a high-speed train derailed in southern Spain, its rear carriages going into the path of a state-run Renfe train, claiming the lives of 46 people.

title: VHS tapes and computers handed to police as Thomas Markle is investigated
summary: The BBC's Jonathan Head is in Cebu, reporting from outside the home where Markle resided.
paragraphs: Watch: VHS tapes and computers handed to police as Thomas Markle is investigated

A court in the Philippine city of Cebu has approved a warrant permitting police to examine material taken from the former home of Thomas Markle, father of the Duchess of Sussex, which is alleged to contain images showing the sexual abuse of children.
Thomas Markle has strongly denied possessing any child abuse material.
His son, who has been living with him in Cebu, told the police he discovered the material in the house where his father resided before returning to the United States earlier this year.
The BBC's Jonathan Head is in Cebu, reporting from outside the home.

title: 'The internet's a less whimsical place' - YouTuber Jacksepticeye branches out
summary: He got famous playing video games but now you're more likely to see Seán McLoughlin in one.
paragraphs: 'The internet's a less whimsical place' - YouTuber Jacksepticeye branches out
The world's changed a lot since Seán McLoughlin, better known to 31 million subscribers as Jacksepticeye, began making YouTube videos.
He started uploading in 2012, in what many people consider to be the platform's "golden age" when vlogging, video game playthroughs and comedy escapism were all the rage.
Like many in the content creation space, he's been branching out in recent years, taking more acting jobs and getting involved in film production.
BBC Newsbeat caught up with McLoughlin to talk about his new role, his work on bringing one of his favourite video games to the big screen and why he misses the "whimsical" days of the internet.
McLoughlin got famous playing video games, and these days there's a good chance you'll see - or hear - him in one.
After a role in the 2025 superhero adventure Dispatch, McLoughlin's got a new role in Hitman, the successful "assassination simulator" from Danish studio IO Interactive.
He plays controversial content creator Finn Colton, known as Finnvictus.
Although the fictional character shares McLoughlin's likeness and voice, he says the "manosphere-adjacent influencer" is not based on him.
As the name of the game suggests, players aren't there to collab with him.
He's one of the celebrity "elusive targets" Hitman's developers occasionally place in the game to encourage returning fans.
"If you love me it'll be funny to play and you'll get to kill me in different ways," says McLoughlin.
"If you hate me maybe that's even more fun to play."
It's not the first time McLoughlin's worked with IO - he appeared, briefly, in their James Bond game 007: First Light earlier this year.
He'd hoped to watch other streamers react to the blink-and-you'll-miss-it cameo, but says many of his friends missed it.
"This time you're forced to interact with me," he says, even if that does involve thinking of imaginative ways to kill him off.
Earlier this year, McLoughlin was also unveiled as a producer on an animated movie version of Bloodborne, one of the highest-rated video games of all time.
Some parts of its passionate fan base reacted negatively to the announcement, questioning the YouTuber's credentials.
McLoughlin reassured them he's a huge fan of the games and has a tattoo of a Hunter's Mark - one of the game's key items - to prove it.
He's described himself as a "vibe-checker" and sees it as his responsibility to make sure the adaptation is done properly.
"If it feels off, especially with something like Bloodborne, people can feel it immediately, even if they don't know what they're pointing towards," he says.
"They know the game so well that if the atmosphere, or the world, or the vibe feels off, they'll pick up on it pretty fast."
McLoughlin says he's been trying to pick people for the project who have ideally played Bloodborne and "have a feeling" for what it's all about.
"I feel like I have good instincts on what works and what doesn't and what I like and what I don't like," he says.
"So the producing side of it fits a lot more naturally for me right now."
Screen adaptations are a big trend in video games at the moment, but they're not the only thing seizing the industry.
Hitman's new mission lands just weeks before the launch of the hugely-anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.
It won't be released on disc at launch, a move that's arguably accelerated the game industry's move towards digital-only games.
McLoughlin, who fondly remembers PlayStation cases on a bedroom shelf and getting new games for Christmas, says "it would suck to see physical games disappear completely".
"Just in terms of the humanity behind it all, I think it would be a shame to see that stuff disappear because it's a magical experience," he says.
The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in video game development is another hot topic at the moment.
Earlier this month, Epic Games, makers of Fortnite, announced a "pivot" towards using AI as a primary development tool.
Like many players, McLoughlin's opposed to its use.
So no chance of seeing a Jacksepticeye Fortnite skin any time soon?
"I think the chances of that happening were already zero before anything related to that even happened," he says.
"But now it's definitely, definitely unlikely."
Physical games, GenAI and content creators' career moves are sure to generate discourse, and conversations online are another thing McLoughlin thinks have changed since he started out.
He says there's been a "rise of anti-communities", where people will "rush to condemn a film or game before it's even been released".
"I'm just sad that the internet is such an angry place these days," he says.
"It's just zero to a thousand immediately. I think we're just not there in terms of having nuanced discussions about anything.
"But I think that's just endemic of the internet in general."
McLoughlin thinks that could be linked to people's real life worries.
"Right now, it's just people are angry in general, just at the world," he says.
"So it's harder to interact with stuff online these days.
"It's a less whimsical space. But hopefully that's something that can change."
McLoughlin's doing his bit to bring people together in December with his annual Thankmas event.
The fundraiser took a break last year but its returning to raise money for the Make-A-Wish Foundation.
"I think it's a nice little pinprick of light in the middle of everything else going on," he says.
And while he's not afraid to speak his mind, he says he is mindful of letting others do the talking sometimes.
"I'm trying to get better about not giving an opinion about absolutely everything any more," he says.
"Because I think there's too much of that in the world."

title: Island Energy: No plans to remove gas standing charge
summary: The provider said any change would need support from the community, the regulator and government.
paragraphs: Island Energy: No plans to remove gas standing charge

The company which provides energy to households on the Isle of Man said it has no plans to change the charging structure, following announcements in the UK Autumn Budget regarding the removal of standing charges.

On Wednesday, Chancellor John Healy announced the removal of standing charges - fixed daily fees paid regardless of usage - from household gas bills in England, Scotland and Wales, with costs added to the unit rate instead.
Island Energy said any proposed changes would be subject to consultation with the Communications and and Utilities Regulatory Authority (CURA) on the island.
A spokesperson warned removing standing charges may benefit some customers but could see others pay more.
"The cost currently covered by the standing charge would instead be recovered through the unit price of energy," explained an Island Energy spokesperson.
"This means customers who use less energy could save money, while those who use more could see their bills increase."
Islands Energy Group supplies energy to homes and business in Guernsey, Jersey and the Isle of Man.

The gas utility and energy service provider, which serves about 40,000 domestic, commercial, and industrial customers across the three islands, said any change to the charging structure would need to have the clear support of the community, the regulator and government.
Treasury Minister Michael Crowe said his department was reviewing the various measures set out by the chancellor to understand what the implications might be for the island.

"As we look towards the Isle of Man Budget, in February 2027, our priority is to strike the right balance between supporting people and businesses today and maintaining strong, sustainable public finances for the years ahead," he said.
In accordance with the Autumn Statement, the island will extend the reduction in the VAT rate, from 5% to 0% on domestic electricity supplies, until 30 June 2027.
It will also honor the Customs and Excise Agreement with the UK and continue to apply the cut in fuel duty, by 5p per litre, until 30 June 2027.
A reduced duty rate for red diesel, introduced in June until the end of the year, will also be extended to 30 June 2027.

title: Minimum wage increase accepted by minister
summary: A recommendation to increase the minimum wage by 2.8% is agreed by Senator Elaine Millar.
paragraphs: A recommendation to increase the minimum wage has been accepted by the social security minister.

The Jersey Employment Forum's latest report recommended hiking the minimum wage rate to £13.97 per hour from 1 April 2027 - an increase of 2.8% on the current £13.59 in line with the Jersey retail price index (RPI) in June 2026.
Senator Elaine Millar, Minister for Social Security, said she had "decided to accept the forum's recommendations in respect of the main minimum wage and trainee minimum wage rates".
Forum chairwoman Carla Benest said it had been "challenging times" for businesses and employees and "the forum has endeavoured to reflect that in our recommendations".
The report recommended minimum wage rates for year one and two trainees remained at £10.50 and £11.75 per hour respectively for one more year from 1 April.

It also recommended an equivalent increase in the allowances available to employers for accommodation and meals provided to employees earning the main minimum wage rate, which Millar said she accepted.
The minister said: "The forum's report also reflected on the debate about a youth rate and possible changes to the way in which the formal trainee minimum wage policy is currently set.
"I will consider carefully the arguments that have emerged from the forum's consultation exercise, and in particular whether a further consultation on these aspects should take place."

title: Minimum wage rise 'a massive blow' says farmer
summary: Tristan Bennett voices his disappointment in the Budget, describing it as "a lot of tinkering".
paragraphs: Minimum wage rise 'a massive blow' says farmer
A farmer has said the minimum wage increase announced in the Budget would be a "massive blow" for businesses like his.
The 3.9% rise was confirmed by Chancellor John Healey during his speech in the House of Commons on Wednesday.
It was among a raft of measures that he said were designed to help ease the pressures of the cost-of-living crisis by offering people "breathing space".
But Tristan Bennett, of Bennetts Farms in Worcester, said it seemed like "a lot of tinkering and gimmicks" and that he was "disappointed there was not anything substantial".
As well as a dairy farm, he also runs a glamping site and cafe, and said the minimum wage increase would hit them hard.
"That's going to have a massive blow, especially for the cafe side and hospitality, and a lot of the young people," he told BBC Hereford and Worcester.
"We are trying to take on apprentices on the farm but we're finding it so hard now to make it pay."
He said the increase in the small business rate relief threshold from £12,000 to £18,000 would help the glamping side of the business a "little bit".
But Bennett said the disappointment was the lack of relief or reduction in VAT for businesses like his.
"They did it for the pubs," he added. "We were hoping they would have been able to help the rest of the hospitality industry but sadly not."
He said he was "nonplussed" by the Budget and questioned why Labour "have not done anything with such a big majority".
"It just seems to be such a mess with things that need sorting out," Bennett said. "If you can't do it with that thumping majority, how else can you do it?
"I'm just completely despondent, really, about the political class and what they're failing to achieve."
Rachel Buchanan, co-owner of Elderwood Books in Brampton Bryan, Herefordshire, said she was currently challenging the business rate valuation of her premises.
She said her current rate was more than £18,000, but if her challenge was successful, her business would be below that figure, which would be a "relief".
"We're in an area subject to flooding. Tourists come or don't come, so if we have a quiet week in the winter, those business rates still have to be paid," she added.
"Having a much lower, or preferably zero, bill would make a massive difference."
She said a reduction in VAT was a "lovely dream" but she did not expect that to be included in the Budget, which she described as "tinkering around the edges".
"I didn't expect any big changes," she continued, "and here we are back to being reliant on ourselves and making sure we have customers coming through the door to pay those bills."

title: Is the double drop from the Premier League becoming more common?
summary: Back-to-back relegations to the third tier of English football are becoming more common and this season Burnley could make it a hat-trick after Luton Town and Leicester.
paragraphs: Is the double drop from the Premier League becoming more common?
One day Leicester were playing Liverpool in the Premier League, then within 15 months it was Notts County, Burton Albion and MK Dons in League One.
It is a path of back-to-back relegations to the third tier of English football which was exceptionally rare. Now statistically it is becoming more common.
With Burnley marooned in the Championship relegation zone, they could be the third team in three years to suffer the double drop,
For the 1,450 Burnley supporters who made the trip to Lincoln City last weekend, the threat is all too real.
Head coach Nicky Hayen was never likely to survive a 4-1 defeat by a Lincoln team who were in non-league football 10 years ago.
With Diego Lopez appointed as Burnley's new chief football officer, and Fabio Celestini installed as their new boss, the Clarets must now hope for a change in fortunes.
Is the Championship becoming ever-more competitive as well-run clubs like Lincoln make an impact?
Or it simply a case of clubs from the Premier League imploding after relegation?
'Mismanagement of the playing squad' to blame
Fifteen years ago, the suggestion a top-flight club could be relegated in successive seasons was unthinkable.
After all, in the first 20 seasons of the Premier League it happened just the once.
That was to Swindon Town, and even then there were special circumstances.
The Robins finished fourth bottom of the second tier in 1994-95 but were relegated because of the rebalancing of the divisions to reduce the Premier League to 20 teams.
In any other season they would not have suffered the double drop.
As such, it could be argued that Wolves were the first team to suffer a double drop from the Premier League after being relegated in 2011-12.
Since then it has happened four times in 14 seasons.
Or, after Sunderland went down in 2016-18, three times in nine seasons.
And then back-to-back seasons with Luton and Leicester.
Meanwhile, Wigan and Portsmouth were relegated to League One after a second season in the Championship, Leeds and Sheffield Wednesday after a third.
For Wolves, Sunderland and Leicester there was considerable turmoil on and off the pitch which contributed to their demise.
Burney fans may fear there are similarities at Turf Moor.
During their double drop descent, Wolves - who remarkably suffered a treble drop to the bottom tier in the 1980s - burned through four managers and made a series of poor transfers.
Sunderland did so with the ignominy of being the only club to finish bottom of both divisions, winning just 13 of 84 league matches.
The Black Cats had been in the top flight for 10 seasons - though they had only reached the 40-point barrier, usually the target to remain in the division, three times.

Leicester's relegation to League One was a direct result of poor boardroom decisions, with a six-point deduction for breaching profit and sustainability regulations ultimately sealing their fate. The Foxes finished 23rd in the Championship, five points from safety.

It took Sunderland four years to return to the Championship, and such is the turmoil at Leicester an immediate promotion looks unlikely. Russell Martin's Leicester side sit 11th in League One, with the club up for sale.

"Despite the fact we've seen Luton and Leicester suffer back-to-back relegations in recent years, I don't see it as a trend that will continue," former Watford and Reading midfielder Jobi McAnuff, now an EFL pundit, told BBC Sport.
"For both of those clubs, in my opinion, it was a case of mismanagement of the playing squad.

"From Luton's perspective, there were a few players there who maybe felt an entitlement to stay in the Premier League. They didn't readjust to being back at the Championship, where most of their players had actually been previously.
"And for Leicester City, they kept hold of too many that didn't really want to be there and then obviously weren't equipped to deal with a relegation battle."
While Luton may have got their recruitment wrong, they were much more responsibly run compared to the other double drop clubs.

The Hatters' progress off the pitch remains progressive rather than regressive, with work advancing on a new 25,000-capacity stadium at Power Court which is due to be completed for the start of 2028-29.

The fine line for success is shown by Luton's relegation from the Championship in 2024-25. They went down because of their inferior goal difference compared to Hull City, with the Tigers then promoted to the Premier League the following season.
Championship will become 'a much more competitive league'
Burnley had earned a reputation as the archetypal yo-yo club - relegated from or promoted to the top division in each of the past five seasons.

But after a leveraged buyout by Alan Pace's ALK Capital in 2020, the Clarets were carrying £142m in loans in the 2024-25 accounts - the year they went up - which was the highest debt level in the Championship.
This week Burnley set a new English league record for the longest run without a home win. When they host Portsmouth on Saturday, it will be 378 days since their last home victory.
Being humbled by a well-run, up-and-coming club like Lincoln, with far fewer resources but savvy ownership, will not be lost on Burnley supporters.
Burnley's total revenue for 2024-25 was £71.7m, which dwarfed Lincoln's £7.81m.
The Clarets then received £48m in parachute payments. Lincoln can expect about £5.5m in solidarity funding.
Off the pitch there should be no contest, but football is not played purely on balance sheets.

In its State of the Game report, published earlier this month, the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) said a new financial deal between the Premier League and the EFL must "reduce the distortive impact that parachute payments have on financial incentives within the Championship".
The solution is merit payments, which would mirror the Premier League's model of prize money by final league position.
At present, every club in the Championship receives the same payment, regardless of where they finish.
"The amount of money paid in parachute payments will reduce and the amount of money going into the Championship will vastly increase," IFR chair David Kogan said.
"The delta between parachute payment clubs and non-parachute payment clubs is going to significantly reduce, which makes the Championship a much more competitive league."
Parachute payments are paid to clubs relegated from the Premier League to help them adjust to the financial realities of the second tier - £48m in year one, then £39m in year two,
Could this make the double drop more common as the revenue gap closes? Much will depend upon just how "significantly" the gap is closed.

The IFR report found that parachute payment clubs were more than four times more likely to be promoted. In 2024-25, four clubs were in receipt and they were almost 27 points better off, and filled the top three places (with Luton relegated).
"If you look at the numbers of teams that go back up or finish in the top places, there's a huge correlation between those clubs and the ones that are parachute payment clubs," McAnuff said.
"Even with a reduction in parachute payments, I still feel that advantage will prove to be massively significant for those teams."
It may yet be that Burnley escape the double drop, that the financial advantage of parachute payments outweighs poor decision-making.
But the double drop has generally become far more common. And that should concern any club that gets relegated and is not prepared for life in the Championship.
body:
One day Leicester were playing Liverpool in the Premier League, then within 15 months it was Notts County, Burton Albion and MK Dons in League One.

It is a path of back-to-back relegations to the third tier of English football which was exceptionally rare. Now statistically it is becoming more common.

With Burnley marooned in the Championship relegation zone, they could be the third team in three years to suffer the double drop,

title: If I Were in My 20s, I'd Buy This 1 ETF Warren Buffett Recommended and Hold It for Decades
summary: In a Berkshire Hathaway letter over a decade ago, Buffett made it clear which fund he likes.
paragraphs: In his 2013 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders, Warren Buffett laid out the advice he'd give to the advisor of his wife's inheritance:
My advice to the trustee could not be more simple: Put 10% of the cash in short-term government bonds and 90% in a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund. (I suggest Vanguard's.)
He didn't offer this advice specifically for retail investors, but I think it obviously applies. And it's a pretty clear endorsement of the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -0.43%).
While it may not sound like the most exciting investment strategy in the world, over time it's proven to be one of the most effective for anyone with a multi-decade time horizon.
Why the S&P 500 makes sense for a 20-something investor
The biggest advantage of the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF is that it gives you exposure to hundreds of the U.S. economy's biggest, most successful companies.

It's tempting to want to put your money straight into growth, tech, and artificial intelligence (AI) stocks. But the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.48%) is one of the best foundational pieces you can own for long-term investing. Only when you have that in place should you start looking at other sector or thematic options.

In the case of the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF, its razor-thin 0.03% expense ratio means that almost every penny your investment earns stays in your pocket. This is especially important if you're in your 20s and potentially holding your investment for four decades or more. Even small differences in expense ratios can add up to thousands of dollars over the long term.

The other big plus of investing in the S&P 500 is that it evolves. Its market cap-weighted methodology means that larger companies receive greater weight in the index. Half a century ago, names like AT&T and General Motors were among the largest holdings in the S&P 500. Today, it's companies like Apple and Microsoft. Over time, the index will change as the economy changes.
A few things to be mindful of when investing in the S&P 500

The tech bull market of the past few years has made the index historically top-heavy. The top 10 holdings alone make up nearly 40% of the index, and the tech sector accounts for 40%. That makes it riskier that a reversal of the current tech rally could sink the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF faster than something like an equal-weight S&P 500 fund that isn't so concentrated.

Also, this is designed to be a long-term holding. That means buying and holding for at least 10 years. The S&P 500 can be volatile, and 20%-plus pullbacks aren't that uncommon. This is normal behavior and should be expected.
What's not a good idea, however, is trying to buy and sell your investment based on short-term events. That tends to hurt long-term returns more than it helps.

If you're buying the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF, make automatic monthly investments to make your account grow faster and avoid the temptation to try to time the market. If you do that for the next 40 years, don't be surprised if you're sitting on a $1 million nest egg when you get to retirement.

title: Russell Brand's wife tells his rape trial he is 'kind and a wonderful father'
summary: Laura Brand tells the jury at his trial she feels "very seen by him" and "I love him very much".
paragraphs: Russell Brand's wife tells his rape trial he is 'kind and a wonderful father'
- Warning: This story contains graphic content.
Russell Brand's wife Laura has told a court her husband is "caring, kind and a wonderful father to our children".
The 39-year-old told the jury at his rape and sexual assault trial that "the way he treats me is to know me", adding: "I feel very seen by him... I love him very much."
The media personality faces seven charges - three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.

Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Thursday, Laura Brand was asked by the defence barrister if her husband respected her when she didn't want to be sexual with him, and she replied: "Yes absolutely."
Laura Brand is the daughter of former golfer Bernard Gallacher and sister of TV presenter Kirsty Gallacher. She married Brand in 2017 and they have three children.
She told the court she first met him at the Edinburgh festival in 2006, explaining that he took her number and they started a relationship soon afterwards.
She said that after his performance: "I went over and said, 'I'm Laura, Kirsty's sister. That was a great show'."
He contacted her the next day, she said. When they met, she said they had oral sex, adding: "He might have wanted to have sex but I didn't want to."
You can follow the trial day by day on the BBC podcast Russell Brand on Trial - available on BBC Sounds, YouTube, iPlayer, or wherever you get your BBC podcasts
Laura Brand said she knew before they met that "he liked women", and found out that while they were dating that he had been having sex with others.
"I wasn't interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people", she said.
"I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other, but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous."
She said she remained friends with Brand while he was married to singer Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012, and got back together with him in 2015.
Asked if she was "aware of his promiscuity" during their time apart, she said: "I was very aware of it. I could read about it regularly in the papers, so I was aware of it and he also told me."
Turning to their relationship now, she said: "We have a very honest, frank, and clear relationship and marriage.
"It is one of the most important parts of our marriage, and our relationship has always been honest."
The charges against Brand relate to allegations made by six female complainants spanning a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.
The entertainer has displayed little emotion during the course of his trial, but was seen smiling broadly during parts of his wife's evidence.
He let out a laugh when she told the court: "We do have many friends and there are colleagues, and we are grateful for those people."
Her evidence came a day after the star appeared in the witness box himself.
He told the jury the allegations had a "devastating" impact on his relationships with friends and colleagues, meaning they would not touch him "with a bargepole".
He also said on Wednesday he had been promiscuous but believes sexual consent is "fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself".
On Thursday, the court also heard statements from two of Russell Brand's ex-girlfriends
Elia Alvarez Diaz said they were in a relationship and lived together for about a year from 1998 to 1999, and described the defendant as "gentle" and "loving".
She described him as being "highly persuasive... a complex character" and "exciting to be with".
"When I said no, however, he accepted it," she said in a statement.
Their relationship ended because he cheated on her repeatedly, she said.
Amanda Alguero Alejos told the court in a statement that Brand had also repeatedly cheated on her.
"He was undoubtedly promiscuous, never in front of me and never when I was around. That was not what mattered to me at the time," she said.
She recalled women "circling" around Brand "like birds", even when they were out as a couple.
The trial continues, with the jury likely to retire to consider the verdicts on Tuesday.

title: I earn £30,000. I'm angry there was no fuel duty cut in the Budget
summary: People on a range of incomes from £4,062 to £150,000 a year tell the BBC what they made of this year's Budget.
paragraphs: I earn £30,000. I'm angry there was no fuel duty cut in the Budget
Chancellor John Healey has unveiled his first Budget.
He announced £100 energy payment for millions and a tax rise on banks, among other measures.
BBC News has been speaking to people on a range of incomes on how they feel about their finances and how the Budget affects them.
Dave Herbert is a professional driver on £30,000 a year. He moves cars between showrooms and does deliveries and says fuel prices have been "crazy" this year.
He spends around £350 a month on petrol for work and personal use. That's 40% to 50% more than at the start of the year, he says.
He has to commute into Cardiff, a 62-mile round trip from his home in Ynysddu. "I'd love to have a hybrid car but even an entry-level used car is too expensive."
The 48-year-old, who is married with a 12-year-old daughter, says he has to find the extra money for fuel "from an already tight budget" and "dreads" filling up at the pump.
The only measure Dave wanted to see was a cut to fuel duty, and he was disappointed this didn't happen.
"I'm pretty angry, really. Nothing has been thrown my way," he says.

The main fuel duty rate has been frozen at 52.95p per litre until the summer, but Dave says: "It sounds like they're giving us something by keeping it frozen but they're actually still taking it off us."
'I get £4,062 a year. I'm frustrated there's no action on NEETs yet'
Emily Nelson completed her A-levels last year and like thousands of her peers has been unable to find a job since leaving college.
The 19-year-old from Swindon wants to be an animator but in the meantime is applying for retail and sales roles and apprenticeships. Most of the time, she doesn't hear back from potential employers.
"I'm trying my best, it's all you really can do. It's kind of suffocating in a way. You see everyone else managing, and you feel like you're not."
Emily was initially disappointed with the Budget, and then frustrated that the government is waiting for the outcome of a review into youth unemployment before legislating next year.
"I'm glad the government is aware, and that they have a plan," she said. "But it's a bit frustrating that we have to wait a little longer to find out what it is."
However, she adds: "It's not happened today, but it will happen."
She wants to see more funding to businesses so they can take on more young employees. She'd also like to see more money for training and the government's Jobs Guarantee, external scheme extended.

The scheme, being rolled out across England, Scotland and Wales, guarantees fully funded, six-month paid jobs for 18 to 24-year-olds who have been on universal credit and looking for work for 18 months. But Emily thinks people should be eligible after a year.
'I earn £22,000. Cost-of-living help doesn't go far enough'
Robert Portlock, 29, has always lived with his parents in Gateshead and would love to move out. But he doesn't think he can afford to.
Rent would be his biggest concern, he says, explaining that a small flat in his area would cost him about two-thirds of his monthly wage.
"Council tax and energy bills would add to it. Food too. I'd need a TV licence, broadband, my car and some money to socialise. By that point I'd be in the minus."
Robert's biggest expense currently is his car, which he says he needs for his 32-mile round trip to work at Newcastle Airport. But he's paying £750 a month in car finance, insurance, fuel and tax.
The Budget "doesn't go far enough", he says, adding he would have liked to have seen more help with the cost of living, including a cut in fuel duty.
The £100 household energy allowance over a year is less than £10 a month, he says, while action on tariffs on food items will save only £21 a year, or £1.75 per month.
"What am I going to buy with that - a Freddo?"

He would like to get on the housing ladder but for now it feels a distant prospect. The government has announced a scheme to help first-time buyers in England who have a deposit of 2.5%. It also confirmed plans for a new First Time Buyer Isa, external, to replace the Lifetime ISA, which will see the government contribute towards the cost of a first home.
But Robert says neither policy will make much difference to him. "You can't save if you don't have money. They seem to be acting as if inflation hasn't happened."
'I earn £41,000. Energy support will definitely help'
Chloe Chin-Saad's husband passed away four years ago and her biggest worry is the cost of living.

She's very grateful that the rent she pays on her south London maisonette is set below the market rate as it is housing association accommodation, but says life was easier when she shared the bills. "Two incomes make a massive difference."
She lives with her 16-year-old son, and says her energy bill has risen sharply over the past year and she now pays about £200 a month on gas and electricity.
"We try to be more aware, we think more about how long we run the hot water when we do the dishes."
Chloe, 40, and her son have cut back on luxuries like going to M&S and the cinema, and she now tries to limit the weekly food shop to £40.

But she can't do anything to reduce her £200 council tax bill, the £250 a month she pays on car finance, or the amount she spends on medicines for her various health conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis.

Two mobile phone bills, and food and pet insurance for her dog also add to her costs. She says the amount she has left over at the end of each month varies, and sometimes she is left with as little as £50.
Chloe says she is "pretty happy" with the Budget, and that "small changes give me hope".
Cutting standing charges on gas, and the £100 household energy payment for households in council tax bands A to D this winter are "definitely going to help", she says.
"It was quite a thoughtful Budget," she adds. "I can see, in years to come, light at the end of the tunnel."
'I earn £150,000. Higher earners like me should've been taxed more'

Jonathan Whitwam, who recently joined the Labour Party, works in finance and says, in addition to his mortgage, his biggest outgoing is supporting his two daughters through university. He and his wife, who live in Essex, pay their rent, which is around £18,000 per year.
His daughters will start their working lives with between £45,000 to £60,000 of debt each, plus interest, which will be compounding at £5,000 to £8,000 per year.

"I have no objection to paying for degrees as I think they are a great way of broadening horizons and having great life experience. But I think the interest should be waived or capped below 1%, otherwise it's a noose around their neck for a substantial part of their lifetime."
Jonathan, 52, says the Budget was "very safe", reducing energy costs for his household by getting rid of standing charges, while cutting bills for many people this winter.
However, he wanted taxes to be put up for higher earners like himself in the name of "redistribution" and says there was "nothing" in the Budget on that.
"If we want better roads, hospitals, schools we need to raise more tax," he adds.
'I have a £15,000 pension. I'm even Stevens after the Budget'
Christine Morris, from Worksop, has been retired for eight years and lives on a state pension combined with a small private pension her late husband left her.
"It is very difficult to balance the books," the 78-year-old says. "I do go on holiday, but I'm spending more of my savings to live."

The chancellor said standing charges would be removed from gas bills, but Christine, who has a gas boiler, says it's not clear yet whether she will benefit, because those costs will be added on to the unit rate.
However, she says the £100 household energy payment will help over the winter
"I'm not sure I'll be better off," she says. Instead she thinks she will be "even Stevens".

She was unconvinced by Andy Burnham's pledge to end the triple lock so that from 2030 the state pension will rise at least by inflation or 2.5%, with the money saved used to create a free-at-the-point of use national care service for England sometime "in the next parliament".
Christine thinks the new service will take time to come in. In the meantime, she fears she will "get less pension and still have to pay out the same for any care I need".
What are you hoping for from the Budget? What questions do you have?

He announced £100 energy payment for millions and a tax rise on banks, among other measures.

BBC News has been speaking to people on a range of incomes on how they feel about their finances and how the Budget affects them.

title: US sanctions Rwanda's defence ministry over DR Congo conflict
summary: Congo accuses Rwanda of backing M23 rebels and plundering minerals in its conflict hit East
paragraphs: US sanctions Rwanda's defence ministry over DR Congo conflict

The United States has imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its alleged support for the M23 rebel group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, increasing pressure on Kigali to withdraw its troops and halt support for the rebels.
"Rwanda must halt its support for M23 and withdraw its troops from eastern DRC," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
The sanctions come months after Rwanda and DR Congo signed a US-brokered peace agreement aimed at ending the conflict.
Fighting has continued in eastern DR Congo since early 2025, when M23 seized the cities of Goma and Bukavu. Rwanda denies backing M23.
The US Treasury says Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.

The M23 has seized mineral-rich areas, including gold-mining sites in South Kivu and Rubaya, a major coltan-producing area in North Kivu. Washington says minerals from rebel-held territory enter Rwanda's supply chains, alleging that Rwanda exports more minerals than it produces.
- Inside the Congolese mine vital to mobile phones, as rebels give BBC rare access
- The evidence that shows Rwanda is backing rebels in DR Congo

The sanctions are intended to reinforce the Washington Accords, signed by the Congolese and Rwandan presidents in December 2025 under US mediation. The deal aimed to end the conflict and expand regional trade and investment, but fighting has continued.
On 24 October, ahead of the sanctions announcement, DR Congo President Félix Tshisekedi urged the international community to increase pressure on Rwanda.
"We must firmly demand that the international community impose concrete sanctions against Rwanda and exert increased pressure, so that we may finally secure a lasting peace in our country," he said.

In a statement to Reuters, DR Congo foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions and urged Rwanda to honour its commitments under the Washington Accords, respect the UN Charter and withdraw its troops from Congolese territory.

"The Washington Accords contain clear commitments regarding Rwanda's security, specifically the neutralization of the DR Congo-sponsored FDLR genocidal militia, which are wholly unmet, and with no accountability," Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo told the BBC.
The FDLR is a militia linked to perpetrators of Rwanda's 1994 genocide. Kigali considers it a security threat and cites its presence in eastern DR Congo to justify its military posture.

"Rwanda remains ready to fully implement the Washington Accords, concurrently with the willingness of the DRC to fulfill those commitments, and with the mediator holding all parties accountable," she said.
The US also sanctioned Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a popular bank and financial institution serving Rwanda's security services.

Washington alleges it facilitated tens of millions of dollars in transactions for M23 and its political wing, the Congo River Alliance, helped pay for military equipment for Rwandan forces from China and enabled gold to be transported from rebel-controlled areas to Kigali.

The sanctions freeze the designated entities' assets under US jurisdiction and generally prohibit US individuals and businesses from conducting transactions with them, unless authorised or exempt. Violations can result in penalties for US and foreign parties.

The measures follow earlier US sanctions against Rwanda's army and four senior military commanders in March 2026. The US imposed further sanctions on Gasabo gold refinery and three mining companies accused of smuggling conflict minerals in June 2026.

Pressure is also mounting over Rwanda's international sports partnerships. Two US senators have urged the National Basketball Association (NBA) to reconsider its commercial relations with Kigali, questioning whether it aligns with the league's stated commitment to human rights.

In a letter sent to NBA commissioner Adam Silver on 23 October, senators Jeff Merkley and Marsha Blackburn questioned the league's continued partnership with Rwanda amid allegations of human rights abuses.
The NBA has yet to issue a substantive response to the letter.
Rwanda has used sports high-profile sports sponsorship to raise its international profile. Early this month, it secured a 10-year deal to host Formula 1's African Grand Prix in the early 2030s.
The country's sponsorship of Arsenal ended in 2026, while Bayern Munich has also ended its commercial partnership with Visit Rwanda.

The M23 has recently joined a new rebel coalition, known as the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) and led by former Congolese President Joseph Kabila, which wants to oust Tshisekedi's government.

"Rwanda must halt its support for M23 and withdraw its troops from eastern DRC," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.

The sanctions come months after Rwanda and DR Congo signed a US-brokered peace agreement aimed at ending the conflict.

title: Elke Sommer, ‘Pink Panther’ and ‘The Prize’ Star, Dies at 85
summary: Elke Sommer, the German-born actress who starred in movies like “A Shot in the Dark,” “Boy, Did I Get the Wrong Number,” “And Then There Were None” and more ’60s and ’70s Hollywood films, died Wednesday at her home in Los Angeles, her stepson Sebastian Walther confirmed to German outlet Bild. She was 85.
paragraphs: Elke Sommer, the German-born actress who starred in movies like “A Shot in the Dark,” “Boy, Did I Get the Wrong Number,” “And Then There Were None” and more ’60s and ’70s Hollywood films, died Wednesday at her home in Los Angeles, her stepson Sebastian Walther confirmed to German outlet Bild. She was 85.
She died just three months after her husband, Wolf Walther, died of cancer. “Now she can finally be with her beloved husband again,” Sebastian Walther told Bild.

Sommer was born in Berlin on November 5, 1940, while it was under Nazi occupation. Her family fled the capital during World War II and relocated to the small town of Niederndorf. In 1957, Sommer moved to London and became an au pair for the family of actress Vicki Michelle. While on holiday in Italy, Sommer was noticed by director Vittorio De Sica and soon started appearing in films. She moved to Hollywood in the early ’60s and became a popular pin-up model.

Sommer starred in major 1960s films like “The Prize” with Paul Newman; the “Pink Panther” sequel “A Shot in the Dark” with Peter Sellers; “The Art of Love” with James Garner and Dick Van Dyke; “The Oscar” with Stephen Boyd; “Boy, Did I Get a Wrong Number!” with Bob Hope; “Deadlier Than the Male”; “The Wrecking Crew” with Dean Martin and Sharon Tate; and “The Wicked Dreams of Paula Schultz.” In 1964, Sommer won a Golden Globe for most promising newcomer actress for “The Prize.”
In the ’70s, her films included “Zeppelin” with Michael York, the Agatha Christie adaptation of “Ten Little Indians,” “Baron Blood,” “Lisa and the Devil” and the British comedy “Carry On Behind.”

title: Original ‘Hunger Games’ Star Elizabeth Banks Praises ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ as ‘Amazing’: Joseph Zada Is a ‘Perfect’ Haymitch
summary: Elizabeth Banks has given two thumbs to “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”
paragraphs: Elizabeth Banks has given two thumbs to “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”

“I’ve seen the film, and it’s amazing,” Banks, who played Effie Trinket in the first four movies of the “Hunger Games” franchise from 2012-2015, told me Wednesday night at the Airbnb.org Gala in Los Angeles.

Based on Suzanne Collins’ 2025 novel “Sunrise on the Reaping,” the new movie centers on a young Haymitch (Joseph Zada, taking over the role from Woody Harrelson) as he fights to survive while competing in the 50th Hunger Games. The cast also features Jesse Plemons as Plutarch, Ralph Fiennes as President Snow, Kieran Culkin as Caesar Flickerman, Elle Fanning as Effie Trinket, Maya Hawke as Wiress and Kelvin Harrison Jr. as Beetee. New characters in the film franchise are played by the likes of Mckenna Grace, Glenn Close and Whitney Peak, among others.
Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson and Woody Harrelson return as Katniss, Peeta and Haymitch in a flash-forward scene.
“Joseph is a perfect Woody Harrelson,” Banks said. “He’s fantastic. I can’t wait for people to see it.”

Earlier this month, I talked to Zada about his work on the movie. His first day filming took place on the Cornucopia. “You’re sitting there and there are 47 other kids around, and there’s a this massive drone, so there’s no crew,” he said. “It was the most mental place to film. Getting ready to run into it, I had all those nerves and it worked out for the character.”
He recalled sharing scenes with Plemons. “He’s so good, and once you get into a little bit, he’s so easy to play with that you really feel like you’re on fire in the moment.”

Close proved to be a jokester at times. “She would growl at me,” Zada said, laughing. “She was so lovely all the time, [but] she’d flip into the character and she’d look at you and hiss. You’re just startled. Just for fun, just to mess with people, I guess.”
He added, “She’s the most wonderful person ever, so generous outside of acting as well. Just always wanted to come up to me and talk and see how I was doing. She’s gorgeous.”
“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” opens in theaters Nov. 20 from Lionsgate.

title: 'I live with a ghost': The people saving money by moving into Japan's haunted houses
summary: Properties where someone has died in tragic circumstances can have big reductions in price.
paragraphs: 'I live with a ghost' - inside the haunted homes attracting bargain hunters
From the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted.
"When I visited the place for a viewing there was a man standing there, glaring at me," she says.
"Since the estate agent couldn't see him, I realised he must be a ghost."
While someone more squeamish would probably have quickly left the flat never to return, Ryua chose to go ahead and move in.
"I'm a bit of a contrarian, so I decided I wanted to become friends with this glaring male ghost," adds Ryua, who works as an aidoru, a young entertainer, and who doesn't wish to share her surname.
Four years later, and still in the same apartment, she says she continues to experience paranormal activity on a daily basis. She says she hears endless footsteps and the ghost talking.

Although Japan has increasingly marked Halloween, external in recent years, many Japanese people take ghosts seriously all year round. The country has a word, "yuurei", which means a lingering, troubled spirit.

These are the ghosts of people who died in violent or tragic circumstances - those who were murdered, killed themselves, or simply were lonely and died alone. If they died at home, then the belief is that their yuurei won't go away.

For house hunters who are not superstitious or squeamish it means there are big bargains to be found. There is a whole category of dwellings called jiko bukken, which means "stigmatised" or "incident" properties.
Under guidelines issued by the government in 2021, Japanese estate agents must disclose suicide, murder, death by fire, and any death where the body was not discovered for an extended period of time.
For rental properties this information must be disclosed for three years, and it must be revealed indefinitely for any property offered for sale.

By contrast, in the UK there is no legal requirement, external to reveal that a person died in a property. And in the US, it differs from state to state., external For example, in California you have to reveal if a person has died in the property in the past three years, while in Arizona and Oregon you do not.

Ryua was told that a man had killed himself in her apartment. It meant that she gets an almost 30% discount on her rent on her tiny, 25 sq m bedsit in the fashionable ward of Setagaya. She says she pays 45,000 yen ($285; £213) a month, instead of what should have been 62,000 yen.

While a house where there had been a murder or suicide would probably be harder to sell or rent out anywhere in the world, Tokyo estate agent Erik Oskamp says that Japanese people are particularly superstitious and averse to stigmatised properties.

"[Even] an apartment next to a cemetery will be difficult to rent out, especially if you can see the tombs from the kitchen," explains Oskamp. "The worst thing is if a suicide has happened in the apartment. Even if somebody has jumped from the roof, many renters will move out. Other issues are a serious crime or a lonely death."
The latter issue, that of a person dying alone, would not generally affect the price of a property in, say, the UK or the US.
But in rural Kagoshima, in Japan's southwest, it enabled Diane Tincher to buy a large three-bedroom house for about half of what would have otherwise been the asking price.

The 79-year-old American has lived in Japan for nearly 40 years, working as a tour guide. She says that the estate agent had been straight with her – there was a heavy discount as an elderly lady had died alone, thereby stigmatising the property.
Tincher paid 20m yen for the house, in a location where similar properties usually sell for up to 45m yen.
"I don't believe in ghosts. But I know that the Japanese are very superstitious," she says. "If there is a ghost I'm thankful to her every day... to live in such a splendid and affordable home."

Researching the house, Tincher had found it on a website called Oshimaland, which lists jiko bukken properties, giving details of the events that occurred. It was launched in 2005 covering Tokyo, before expanding across Japan and then internationally in 2011.
It is crowdsourced, meaning that members of the public add the homes and their details.
Teru Oshima, the founder of Oshimaland, says that in the past such properties were "not very attractive options" in Japan.

Yet as house prices have surged in the country in recent years, as well as a big increase in the wider cost of living, one 2025 survey found that more than half of Japanese people would now rent a jiko bukken if it was cheap., external
Back in Setagaya, Ryua says she is happy living with her ghostly flatmate. "I believe that ghosts were once living human beings, so they deserve our respect," she says.

title: Audacious Indian jailbreak saga ends with 17 prisoners recaptured
summary: The jailbreak began with a fake seizure and ended 36 hours later with all the inmates back behind bars.
paragraphs: Audacious Indian jailbreak saga ends with 17 prisoners recaptured
A fake medical emergency, an audacious jailbreak and a 36-hour search operation that ended with 17 prisoners being recaptured.
Those are the highlights of a story from India's Tamil Nadu state that has captured headlines across the country.
It began on Monday night after 17 men escaped from a prison in Theni district in the southern state after overpowering guards, and ended almost two days later with police catching them in batches.

The incident has drawn attention to overcrowding in Indian prisons. Police say the Theni prison was housing 334 inmates against a capacity of 200, leaving authorities unable to maintain control once chaos broke out.
The state police said it has suspended nine staff at the prison for alleged negligence in connection with the incident.
All the men who escaped were undertrials - inmates on trial or awaiting one - and 18 of them were in one cell at the prison in Thekkampatti in Theni.

On Monday night at 2230 local time (17:00 GMT), one of the prisoners acted like he was going through a seizure. The other cellmates shouted for help and a jail official responded. He was soon overpowered by the prisoners, police said.

The prisoners then got out of the cell, reportedly attacked two other jail guards and took away keys which they used to open the main gate and flee. While 17 escaped, one returned to the prison immediately.
Several prison personnel were injured in the attack.
Police sources told BBC Tamil that they were examining the possibility of collusion between some prison officials and the escaped men.
Sandeep Rathore, Director General of Police for Prisons in Tamil Nadu, said in a press briefing that the jailbreak was caused by "human error".
"There was a clear breach of security protocol as the prisoners managed to pass through a three-tier barrier manned by security personnel," he said.
On Thursday, he was replaced as the head of state prisons and transferred to a different department.

At the time of the incident, only four guards were on duty, far below the staffing required to maintain the prescribed 1:6 guard-to-inmate ratio recommended by the state - which should have worked out to 34 guards against the approved strength of 200 prisoners.
The police then launched a manhunt, calling forces from across the state.
"Advanced technology, drone surveillance, CCTV footage analysis, and the tireless efforts of police personnel played a crucial role," the department said in a statement on X.
Four men were arrested at a bus station in a nearby village, and the fifth was caught while he was travelling in a tuk-tuk.

A drone search of a forest near the prison led to eight more escaped prisoners being caught. Videos of the arrests showed the men obeying police instructions even as they did not answer questions from reporters who were also seen at the scene.
Two more were captured with the help of drone surveillance, police said, while the last two men surrendered on Wednesday.
News agency PTI reported that all 17 recaptured prisoners have been moved to high-security correctional prisons.
Rathore told media that all prisons across the state would be audited to check if rules were being followed.

The incident evoked memories of one of the biggest jailbreaks in Tamil Nadu in 1995 when 43 suspected militants escaped from a special camp after digging a 153-foot-long tunnel beneath a historic fort. Some of them were never recaptured.

While the investigation is going on, the incident has sparked a conversation on overcrowding in Indian prisons. The National Crime Records Bureau's last Prison Statistics India report from 2023 showed a national occupancy rate of 120.1%.

Data shows that undertrial prisoners - individuals who are detained while they await police investigation or court trials - make up more than 73% of India's total prison population. Human rights groups and legal experts have also raised concerns about delays in investigations and trials that lead to people languishing for years behind bars.
Additional reporting by Siraj and Prabhurao Anandhan

title: Hello Kitty maker cuts ties with Japanese spy drama after China backlash
summary: Sanrio has apologised after its merchandise line with Japanese TV series Vivant drew criticism.
paragraphs: Hello Kitty maker cuts ties with Japanese spy drama after China backlash
Sanrio, the company behind Hello Kitty, has apologised and ended its merchandise partnership with a controversial Japanese TV show after drawing backlash in China.

Vivant, a popular spy thriller, has been widely slammed in Chinese state media and by Chinese social media users for its depiction of Chinese agents using brutal torture tactics on a Japanese operative.
The criticism has extended to the internationally beloved Hello Kitty and her friends, including My Melody and Cinnamoroll, who were featured in merchandise dressed as characters from the show.
Sanrio said it terminated its collaboration with Vivant after determining that it "contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio's core values".

"Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people," Sanrio said in the statement late on Wednesday.
"We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects."
China-Japan ties have plunged to their lowest point in years, since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan last November sparked a diplomatic firestorm.
Responding to a question in parliament, Takaichi suggested that Japan would activate its self-defence force if China attacked Taiwan.
Beijing has since been heaping pressure on Tokyo, from restricting rare earth exports to curbing tourism and even reclaiming its pandas.
Takaichi told parliament earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and planned to watch them over the year-end holidays.
State-run Global Times took aim at Sanrio on Wednesday, saying the hugely popular cat character "should not dance with Japan's right wing".

Sanrio "stands to lose far more than short-term sales" by collaborating with "anti-China content", the Global Times article said. "The trust and emotional bond it has built up over a long time will also suffer."

When asked about Sanrio's scrapped partnership with Vivant on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry said the incident should "serve as a warning to the international community and discerning people in Japan".
Hello Kitty is not the only internationally beloved figure to have faced such wrath in China in recent days.
Earlier this week, several Chinese brands dropped French footballer Kylian Mbappé over comments he had made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong - which he has since apologised for.
Vivant is about a Japanese salaryman who finds himself entangled in an international web of crime and espionage.

Its first season, which aired in 2023, was set in a fictional Central Asian country. Its second season, which premiered in July, features Chinese agents torturing a Japanese spy by cutting his fingers and stabbing his abdomen.
Chinese state outlets, including CCTV, argued that these tactics "highly overlap" with those historically used by Japanese troops against the Chinese, and that the drama "distorts the truth".
Masamine Ryuho, the president of Vivant's TV network TBS, said on Wednesday that the show was completely fictional and had no intentions of "disparaging any particular country".

Vivant, a popular spy thriller, has been widely slammed in Chinese state media and by Chinese social media users for its depiction of Chinese agents using brutal torture tactics on a Japanese operative.

The criticism has extended to the internationally beloved Hello Kitty and her friends, including My Melody and Cinnamoroll, who were featured in merchandise dressed as characters from the show.
