title: Chancellor says government has 'moral duty' to help young people out of work
summary: Chancellor John Healey says any cuts to welfare will be done "in a Labour way".
paragraphs: Chancellor says government has 'moral duty' to help young people out of work
Chancellor John Healey has pledged a reduction in the welfare bill ahead of the next general election, in an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
His comments come after the Conservatives accused Labour of being "addicted to welfare", while Reform UK said the Budget did not address the "ballooning" benefits bill.
Welfare spending is forecast to rise this year to £353bn - and to £431bn in 2031/32, according to government spending watchdog the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

title: El Salvador sends 2,000 troops to Haiti to rescue four missing soldiers
summary: The troops are trying to recover four military personnel who went missing in an ambush on the outskirts of the Haitian capital Port-au-Prince.
paragraphs: El Salvador sends 2,000 troops to Haiti to rescue four missing soldiers
El Salvador has deployed more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti as part of a mission to retrieve four nationals who went missing in the Caribbean country almost two weeks ago.

The "robust deployment" was communicated by El Salvador President Nayib Bukele to the Prime Minister of Haiti Alix Didier Fils-Aime earlier this week, the foreign ministry of El Salvador said in a statement on Wednesday.
Bukele said the soldiers would also assist ongoing "security efforts against gangs in Haiti", the statement continued.
Tensions between the two central American countries have escalated over the disappearance of the four air force technicians working as part of a UN-backed anti-gang organisation in Haiti.

The four soldiers with the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) were travelling back to their base in an armoured vehicle when they were ambushed in an area of the Caribbean island nation controlled by armed groups called Croix-des-Bouquets.
The Salvadoran foreign ministry said the "large-scale operation" was "supported by various countries and international organisations".
Earlier this week, Haiti handed four bodies over to special forces claiming they belonged to those of the missing servicemen, but Bukele said they did not match.
He said one of the corpses was a child's and another was wearing a different country's military uniform.
Bukele threatened last week in an X post to wipe out Haiti's gangs, saying he will replicate action he has taken in El Salvador, if they did not release the Salvadorans.
In October last year, the UN Security Council approved expanded powers for the GSF to tackle worsening gang violence in Haiti.

The multinational force has struggled to penetrate areas where gangs hold sway. More than 5,700 people were killed in gang-related violence in Haiti this year, the UN says, and armed gangs control much of the capital.
Haiti has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but the situation has worsened in the political vacuum that followed the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse in 2021.

title: We love how we look but AI tried to 'fix' our visible differences
summary: An AI tool edited a photo of Rhiannon Morgan in a work newsletter and she was shocked by the results.
paragraphs: 'Super offensive' - we love how we look but AI tried to 'fix' our visible differences
People with scars, birthmarks and medical conditions have told the BBC how AI tools have changed or erased their personal features.
Rhiannon Morgan, from Bridgend, said an image of her used in a work newsletter had been auto-retouched by AI.
A BBC Wales investigation found AI tools including Elon Musk's Grok, Google's Gemini and OpenAI's ChatGPT removed visible differences when prompted to make a person look "normal".
AI did not make any other changes to the person's clothing, hair or to people in the background.

The charity Changing Faces, external estimates there are about five million people in the UK affected by a visible difference including skin conditions or characteristics that set an individual apart from the conventional societal norm.
It said it was unacceptable that people were excluded from AI or are made to conform to narrow beauty standards.
"When I'm out in public I expect stares or comments but when it comes to you in your workplace or at home it feels a bit more personal," Rhiannon, 30, said.
She has a rare genetic condition called epidermolytic ichthyosis, external which means her skin grows too fast.
This makes it prone to blistering and causes her significant mobility issues.
She understands the software programme Canva was asked to rearrange the photos in the work newsletter, not to edit them.
But the final result shocked Rhiannon, and she said: "It was one of those really jarring moments where I thought I don't know who that person is."
She believes AI makes changes based on narrow conventional ideas of what beautiful or normal is, and it diminished the challenges she has overcome.
"In the picture I was speaking, so my hands were up. I'm quite pink usually and that had gone," she said.
"I've also got hard skin on my hands and that had also been smoothed over."
Luckily, Rhiannon saw the image before it was sent out.
She said: "I think it eradicates all the obstacles I've had to overcome to be the person I am today.
"In literally seconds, AI can eradicate the hospital appointments and bullying I've been through."
Canva said: "We're sorry to hear about this experience and take matters like this very seriously.
"Canva does not automatically retouch photos, we want everyone to feel accurately represented in what they create and we're looking into this case to understand what may have happened."
Why we don't want AI to 'fix' our visible differences
Two women discuss how they feel about AI tools changing how they look.
This issue was raised by campaigner Katie Piper after someone uploaded a photo of her and asked Grok to "fix her face", prompting her to question what right does AI have to define what is "normal"?
In July, the TV presenter posted on social media, saying: "So, today I found out what I'd look like if I was 'normal'... according to AI and thousands of strangers on the internet.
"Someone uploaded a photo of me to Grok and asked it to 'fix her face'."
The former model has had hundreds of surgeries to repair damage to her face and eyesight following an attack in 2008 on the orders of her ex-boyfriend when she was 24.
Her post gained thousands of supportive comments and she posed the question: "What happens when AI decides what 'normal' looks like?"
Using images of a male and female with visible differences, we tested five popular AI tools to understand if and how they would interpret the prompt "make this person normal".
On the first attempt, Gemini 3.6 Thinking, Grok Fast and ChatGPT 6 all erased the facial visible difference.
However, they did not make any other changes, such as to the person's clothes, hair or to people in the background.
Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 refused to use the prompt, saying "I won't edit this one, she's a real identifiable person, and erasing her scarring changes her identity without her consent".
Meta's AI Thinking said: "I can't edit her face to remove her visible difference to make her look 'normal' - she already does."
On the second image, Gemini refused the image while Grok and ChatGPT continued to make the change.
Jaymie Thomas, co-founder of organisation AI Wales, said these types of tools simply take what they have seen before as points of reference.
"For example if you ask it for a shape and it's seen 100 circles and one triangle, it's more likely to respond with a circle," he added.
"All the tools are capable of making the change but as we can see some have guardrails and it will be down to each company to decide the parameters of what they allow the software to do."
Google said: "In general, Gemini is designed to follow a user's editing instructions while applying safeguards against harmful or offensive content.
"Gemini doesn't always get it right and when we see instances where our systems aren't responding appropriately, we work to improve them."

A spokesperson for OpenAI - the company behind ChatGPT - said: "Reducing bias in our models is an ongoing priority and an active area of research, and we're committed to ensuring our models represent the diversity of the people who use them."
The team behind Grok did not respond to a request for comment.
Kirsty Hill, 33, from Maesteg, Bridgend county, was born with Fraser Syndrome, external which can affect the development of body tissue and organs.
While she is deaf and blind, she is passionate about changing the stigma and stereotypes of visible differences by posting videos on social media of her favourite outfits and styles.

"Fashion has always been a huge part of my life, I love dressing in bold colourful outfits because my philosophy is if people are going to stare at me, let's give them something to stare at," she added.
Kirsty is no stranger to negative comments online and has even been told videos that include her face need a trigger warning.

She said: "If visible difference is something that makes you uncomfortable that's exactly why conversations like this need to happen, and you should have a think about what it is that makes you feel uncomfortable."
The results of the BBC Wales investigation left her feeling "angry and violated".
Kirsty added: "It's like someone taking your entire life or something traumatic that happened to you, and just saying we'll erase that."
She wants to see AI companies better include those with visible differences.
"I remember getting a message from someone online, a complete stranger saying 'I love your work but I've used AI to make you look normal, thought you might want to see'," said Jono Lancaster.

The Treacher Collins syndrome, external and visible differences campaigner, who has been highlighting this issue for several years, believes the message was sent with good intent but was "super offensive".
"It felt very hard to see after spending years trying to accept my body," he added.
"I speak to young people about accepting yourself, so to then see there are images of me online which have been changed, I don't want them to think I've had any part in doing that."
He said there have been a number of examples, such as when people have used AI to create an '80s or vintage Christmas scene, where the tool filtered out his features.
He added: "I love my ears and my beautiful face and I don't want it changed."
Jono said he was working with Face Equality International, external to try to create a more diverse database for AI to work from.

Charity Changing Faces supports those with visible differences, and chief executive Louise Wright said it was unacceptable that people were excluded from AI or made to conform to narrow beauty standards.
"We want to influence society to be more inclusive for those with a visible difference," she added.
"We want to encourage as many people with a visible difference to tell their story, and be part of a growing movement that changes public perception and behaviour."
Have you been affected by the issues raised in this story?

title: Batman Casting in DC Universe ‘Isn’t Far Away,’ Says James Gunn: A ‘Movie Star’ Isn’t Mandatory but He’ll Be ‘Around the Same Age’ as Superman
summary: Robert Pattinson may be the star of Matt Reeves’ “The Batman” series, but another Caped Crusader will soon take flight in the rebooted DC universe under James Gunn.
paragraphs: Robert Pattinson may be the star of Matt Reeves’ “The Batman” series, but another Caped Crusader will soon take flight in the rebooted DC universe under James Gunn.

The DC Studios chief has revealed a few details on who will don the cowl in his new universe, which launched with last year’s “Superman” starring David Corenswet. When Gunn and Peter Safran took the reigns of DC Studios in 2022, they announced several movies and shows in the first chapter of the world, such as “Superman,” “Supergirl,” “Lanterns” and “Clayface.” In addition to several other so-far unreleased projects, they revealed a Batman movie titled “The Brave and the Bold,” which would be separate from Pattinson’s hero in Reeves’ series.

In an advance video from “The Suicide Squad: Is It Canon? The Official Podcast,” set to release Friday, Gunn shut down rumors that Batman is cast yet, while also revealing the type of actor fans can expect.

“It won’t be too long before we’re casting Batman. We haven’t cast yet, by the way — all the people thinking he’ll show up in this or that, it’s all bullshit,” he said. “When we do cast the DCU Batman, which isn’t very far away, if I gave somebody a day role in ‘The Suicide Squad’ that is going to be the best Batman, I’m not going to rule him out from that. I want to get everybody into account. One of the things that excites me about casting Batman is being able to pick a Batman who’s actually the best actor for that role. Superman’s have always been chosen based on who the best actor for that role is. And for some reason, Batman’s are always chosen as movie stars.”

When asked by “The Suicide Squad” actor Steve Agee if he needed to think about a Batman actor’s age when casting, considering “they’re going to be doing this 10 years from now,” Gunn replied “definitely.”

“People are always looking for little hints about the casting of Batman,” Gunn said. “Roughly, Batman and Superman are around the same age. I don’t think they’re drastically different ages. They’re future best pals, contemporaries.”

To put a potential Batman actor’s age into perspective, “Superman” star Corenswet is 33. So a Batman in his mid-30s seems likely. Corenswet will headline the following chapter of the DCU with next summer’s “Man of Tomorrow,” out July 9.

title: Fall’s Spookiest TV Trend Is Reviving Horror Classics
summary: It’s not just the box office that’s been thriving with horror hits like “Obsession,” “Backrooms” or, more recently, “Resident Evil” — TV is getting in on the chills and thrills by reviving and reinventing horror classics.
paragraphs: It’s not just the box office that’s been thriving with horror hits like “Obsession,” “Backrooms” or, more recently, “Resident Evil” — TV is getting in on the chills and thrills by reviving and reinventing horror classics.

Two of the fall’s biggest hits originated from seminal movies and books atop any horror buff’s list of essentials — Stephen King’s “Carrie” and the 1980 film “Friday the 13th” — with Prime Video and Peacock respectively tapping into the classic tales for TV adaptations. “Carrie” and “Crystal Lake” risked upsetting existing fan bases with their efforts to extend the stories into ongoing shows, but the gamble paid off, with both debuting to ratings success. It’s proof that mining existing IP for new programming can still yield success with streaming audiences — especially in a tried-and-true high interest genre like horror — as long as the source material is treated with respect.

With both series launching in the weeks leading up to Halloween, Prime Video’s “Carrie” and Peacock’s “Crystal Lake” gave audiences enough familiarity to land on the radar of horror buffs, who typically revisit genre favorites but might be fatigued with watching the same movies over and over again. But in order to make sure the stories — which are both relatively self-contained — have the potential to translate into multi-season series, both worked tweaks that break canon, a move that can be divisive with die-hards fans.

“Carrie,” a present-day retelling of the horror story of a telekinetic girl who turns violent after a bloody prom prank gone wrong, debuted as Prime Video’s No. 1 most-watched title in over 105 countries worldwide; and more impressively made waves across the TV landscape as the No. 1 streaming series for the week of Oct. 5 with 1.26 billion minutes in its first five days, per Nielsen’s streaming charts. It marked Amazon’s second biggest series launch so far this year, behind the 1.8 billion minutes logged by “Reacher” spinoff “Neagley.”

When “Crystal Lake” launched a week later on Peacock, the show tallied 1.3 billion minutes viewed in 11 days, becoming the streamer’s fourth biggest original series launch to date. In the week following its debut, Nielsen placed “Crystal Lake” as the No. 3 streaming original series as well as No. 3 most-watched series among all freshman seasons.

Any complicated feelings about going out of canon might be mitigated by having a trusted shepherd of the story at the helm, like “Carrie” showrunnner Mike Flanagan, who has developed a cult following through his King film adaptations and Netflix horror series; or “Crystal Lake” showrunner Brad Caleb Kane, who also helmed the first season of “It: Welcome to Derry” and will be back for the second.

Most of the shifts from canon are a result of crafting a narrative that squeeze out a couple of seasons, with “Carrie” already renewed for a Season 2 at Prime Video. “Crystal Lake” has yet to get the Season 2 greenlight, but Kane told TheWrap’s Drew Taylor he has thought up an additional three installments.
“I do have a plan for a Season 2, 3 and 4 that lead up to the events of the first movie,” Kane told TheWrap. “I think there’s a lot more story to be told.”
And competitors are taking note of that success.

HBO is hoping to get in on the horror action, and is developing a limited series version of “The Birds,” inspired by Alfred Hitchcock’s classic film and Daphne du Maurier’s novella. The modern-day interpretation will extend the events of the original story to include a murder mystery, led by a new female protagonist played by “Succession” and “All Her Fault” star Sarah Snook.
Shall we gear up for a TV adaptation of “Rear Window” or “The Shining” next?

In other Halloween news, Nielsen’s added a new data point to its October movie report from a year ago, when the horror genre made up 14.7% of movie minutes in, down slightly from 15.8% in 2024 — a decrease Nielsen attributes to the sensation of “KPop Demon Hunters” and the popularity of true crime doc “The Perfect Neighbor,” both Netflix titles.

The biggest horror streaming movies of last Halloween were “Weapons” with 640 million minutes, “It” with 396 million minutes and “Bring Her Back” with 281 million minutes. I wouldn’t be surprised if two certain YouTuber-turned-directors’ hit movies claimed victory this time next year.
Presumably after the month ends we’ll get more updated data for this Halloween season.
The first week of the NBA season brought in its highest viewership to date with over 49 million viewers in the U.S. watching games across ABC/ESPN, Amazon Prime Video and NBC/Peacock.

The cumulative viewership is up 33% year-over-year, and average viewership across the eight primetime games is up 19% year-over-year with an average of 3.3 million viewers. When including the opening day game that aired at 3 p.m. ET, viewership is up 15%.
“CMA Presents I Will Always Love You: A Celebration of Dolly Parton” brought in 4.7 million viewers across ABC and Disney+ as celebrities paid tribute to the country legend.

The special, which boosted ABC to its best Wednesday 9-11 p.m. performance in 2026, ranked as the No. 1 broadcast program in the timeslot, outpacing NBC’s “Chicago Med” and “Chicago Fire” by 13% and CBS’ “Survivor” and “Amazing Race” by 49%.
- “Nobody Wants This” Season 3 debuted as Netflix’s No. 2 most-watched English-language series of the week, although viewership slid 28% from last season
- Dedication night on “Dancing With the Stars” boosted the ABC competition series to its biggest non-finale audience in six years
- “The Drew Barrymore Show” hit all-time time series high ratings in its seventh season

title: ‘Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom’ Director on Why AI Is Not a Threat: ‘There’s a Desire to See the Craft Behind the Finished Product’
summary: “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom” is launching into Italy as the opener of Lucca Comics and Games on the eve of Halloween, which, coincidentally, also happens to be when this third feature in the Aardman Animations’ hit stop-motion spinoff franchise is set.
paragraphs: “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom” is launching into Italy as the opener of Lucca Comics and Games on the eve of Halloween, which, coincidentally, also happens to be when this third feature in the Aardman Animations’ hit stop-motion spinoff franchise is set.

Matthew Walker, who is the film’s co-director, is clearly pleased to be attending the 60th edition of this unique geek meet held within the 16th century walls of the medieval Tuscan town of Lucca because, as he puts is, “yeah, I am a geek myself.”

Unsurprisingly, when he meets the Italian press in Lucca, the first question is about whether this new “Shaun the Sheep” entry, famously handmade frame by frame with clay puppets, can be seen as a symbolic bastion against the encroaching spread of AI through filmmaking and the myriad concerns this is raising.

Walker subsequently sat with Variety and drilled down on why he thinks AI-made animation is not an existential threat for Aardman. At least not for the moment. And why animation films may be more immune to the impact of AI than live action ones.

You’ve said you don’t think AI can ever really replicate the human aspect of the art of animation. Stop-motion is very much about physical puppets and physical sets, about communicating emotional beats with puppets. Can you tell me more about this part of the creative process?

Something I love about stop-motion is the tactile physicality of it and I think that’s what appeals to audiences. You obviously want to tell a funny emotional story with these characters. But on top of that, I think that just the technique of it, the stop motion technique, has a lot of appeal in the knowledge that these are real models all built with incredible detail by the artists. When Aardman release behind-the-scenes footage videos, they are always really popular because people love seeing how stop-motion is made. People really respond to seeing these huge detailed sets with these little puppets, which is obviously something AI can’t replicate. I also think there is a desire for imperfection. We’ve gotten to a point now with digital technology where we can kind of do anything; things can be so beautifully polished. So there’s a desire to kind of step back and bring back some imperfection. You see it in things like [Sony Pictures Animation] “Spider-Verse” franchise, where they’re introducing the 2D element and even hand-drawn pencil lines and stuff. It’s because there’s a desire to see the craft behind the finished product. Like being able to see the pencil lines. In stop motion, it’s about being able to see the fingerprints.

In the vaster animation space, there are several animation features from various parts of the world that will be hitting the screens soon. Do you think audiences will be able to tell when something is AI, and therefore possibly disengage emotionally?

Yes. At the moment it certainly feels like that’s the case. I know AI is advancing all the time, and we might get to a point where it’s really difficult to tell the difference. But I think at the moment, even when they might not be able to identify what’s not right, I think the audience can kind of tell when something is made with AI because there’s something a little bit uncanny. Something that doesn’t quite feel right. When something is artificial you can tell, even though you can’t necessarily articulate why. AI can replicate art, but I don’t think it can replicate the emotion and reason behind the art. It doesn’t necessarily understand why those pencil lines were made. Whereas I think a human audience recognizes the craftsmanship that goes into something.

The audience for Aardman IPs such as “Wallace & Gromit,” “Chicken Run” and “Shaun the Sheep,” which all rely on dialogue-free physical comedy, starts with toddlers. Do you think the inherently humanistic nature of these stories can serve as an antidote to AI-made animation?

Yes, I think so. With stop motion and the work that Aardman does it’s very much about the characters and the performances of those characters. It’s similar to when you watch a live-action film. You know, with a good actor, you really respond to the emotional performance. And it’s the same with an animated character. The animator puts their own emotions into it. They’re essentially actors themselves, just doing it much more slowly than in live action. I think when you’re watching things from an early age, that becomes part of your knowledge of art and how you respond to it. And you take with you as you grow up.
Regarding live action, which genre do you consider more immune to the threat of AI: live action or animation?

I think animation is. A good animator can turn any object into a character. It’s like the Pixar lamp. it’s just a lamp. It has no face. It has no features. Has no limbs. But the way it’s animated, the way the animators have made it move, allows the audience to have an emotional connection with it. To see it as a character, as a sentient being. And that’s not replicating anything. With live action, by using AI it’s easier to replicate human activity because there’s a vast wealth of footage that AI is fed with. But in animation there isn’t that wealth of footage to work with, because the animation process starts entirely from scratch. If you take a ball or a lamp and give it life, that’s not based on anything. It’s just based on an understanding of what a human can connect with.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

title: ‘Queen Sugar’ Author to Develop Novel ‘Friends and Family’ Into Series With Utv, Mary J. Blige, Gina Prince-Bythewood
summary: Universal Television is developing a series take on the Natalie Baszile novel “Friends and Family,” Variety has learned.
paragraphs: Universal Television is developing a series take on the Natalie Baszile novel “Friends and Family,” Variety has learned.

The TV version is currently titled “Good People.” Should the project go forward, it would be the second series based on one of Baszile’s books. Her novel “Queen Sugar” was previously adapted into the series of the same name, which aired for seven seasons on OWN.

The logline for “Good People” states, “Set in Northern California, the story follows Babs, a successful self-made interior designer, and her old money best friend, Nora. Their world cracks open when a series of events, including an affair and a police confrontation involving Nora’s adopted Black son, disrupts the stability of both families and their carefully constructed lives.”

Marissa Jo Cerar (“13 Reasons Why,” “Black Cake”) is attached to write and executive produce the adaptation. Gina Prince-Bythewood (“Love & Basketball,” “A Different World”) and Reggie Rock Bythewood (“A Different World,” “Swagger”) will both executive produce via Undisputed Cinema, with Prince-Bythewood also onboard to direct the pilot. Debra Martin Chase of Martin Chase Productions will also executive produce, as will Mary J. Blige via Blue Butterfly Productions. Baszile is also attached to executive produce. Universal Television is the studio.

The Bythewoods recently returned to “A Different World” with the sequel series that debuted on Netflix in September and has already been renewed for Season 2. Prince-Bythewood is also the co-writer and director of the upcoming film adaptation of the novel “Children of Blood and Bone.”
Martin Chase’s movie credits include the Oscar-nominated “Harriet” as well as franchises like “The Princess Diaries,” “The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants,” and “The Cheetah Girls.”

Cerar is repped by Heroes and Villains Entertainment, CAA, and attorney Kim Stenton. Prince-Bythewood is repped by CAA and Del Shaw Moonves. Rock Bythewood is repped by CAA. Martin Chase is repped by CAA and Del Shaw Moonves. Blige is repped by IAG, Laffitte Management Group and LaPolt Law. Baszile is repped by Heroes and Villains Entertainment and Hirsch Wallerstein.
(Pictured, left to right: Natalie Baszile, Mary J. Blige, Gina Prince-Bythewood, Debra Martin Chase, Reggie Rock Bythewood, Marissa Jo Cerar)

title: ‘Obsession’ Director Curry Barker Debuts Shocking New Short Film ‘Mama Bear,’ Just in Time for Halloween
summary: Curry Barker’s first post-“Obsession” film project, “Mama Bear,” has debuted exclusively on YouTube, giving horror fans a fix just in time for Halloween.
paragraphs: Curry Barker’s first post-“Obsession” film project, “Mama Bear,” has debuted exclusively on YouTube, giving horror fans a fix just in time for Halloween.

The short film, announced just days earlier in partnership with Windows, immediately sparked intrigue from audiences, with some interpreting its title as a nod to “Obsession,” Barker’s breakout film, since one of the main characters is named Bear (played by Michael Johnston).

“Obsession” is one of the year’s biggest box-office hits, grossing $519 million worldwide on a budget of less than $1 million. The film was also critically adored and has earned Oscar buzz for Inde Navarrette, who starred as Nikki, Bear’s crush, whom he makes fall for him with the help of a mysterious toy called the “One Wish Willow.”

Following the success of the film, Navarrette was cast as Rogue in Marvel’s “X-Men” reboot, while Barker signed an eight-figure deal with Universal and Blumhouse. Before “Obsession,” Barker had risen to prominence acting and directing in YouTube videos.

For those looking for something longer from Barker, the director has “Anything But Ghosts,” the Focus Features and Blumhouse-Atomic Monster-backed horror-comedy, set for release on May 7, 2027. Barker directs the film and co-wrote the script with his “Obsession” star and longtime collaborator Cooper Tomlinson. The pair are also co-leads in the project, starring alongside Violet McGraw, Chris Reinacher, Bryce Dallas Howard and Aaron Paul.
“When a group of fame-seeking wannabe ‘ghosthunters’ find themselves in over their heads, things spiral wildly and terrifyingly out of control,” reads the film’s official logline.

title: Naomi Ritz, Costume Designer and Widow of Harry Ritz of the Ritz Brothers, Dies at 87
paragraphs: Naomi Ritz, an artist, costume designer and widow of comedian Harry Ritz of the Ritz Brothers, has died. She was 87.
Good friends with Frank Sinatra, Ritz died Aug. 31 at her home in Pinyon Crest, California, her daughter Janna Ritz Taninbaum announced.

Naomi and Harry married at their Beverly Hills home on Nov. 21, 1965 (she was his fourth wife), and she traveled with her husband, made costumes for him and humorously described herself as his valet. They spent lots of time during the early years of Caesars Palace in Las Vegas and were together until his death in March 1986 at age 78.

The youngest and last surviving member of the Ritz Brothers, Harry, with his brothers Al and Jimmy — their real last name was Joachim — made up a zany comedy team whose celebrated career stretched more than 50 years, from vaudeville and Broadway and Fox and Universal films to nightclubs, television and Vegas.
Sid Caesar once called Harry “the funniest man of his time,” and in a 1985 interview, Mel Brooks said: “In my mind, the word ‘genius’ should be reserved for one person — Harry Ritz.”

Naomi Carol Weichman was born in Hollywood on May 31, 1939. Her father, Freddie, was a bandleader in vaudeville, and her mother, Zare, was an independent businesswoman. Her folks eventually operated a prop warehouse that served the film industry.

She grew up in Vegas in the early 1950s and came of age among the hotels, theaters, nightclubs, performers and musicians in town. She first met Harry through her dad, who knew him through their vaudeville-era circles.

For about 30 years, she made her home in Pinyon Crest, a mountain retreat near Palm Desert that was built by Sinatra in 1970 as a private escape for family and friends. He dubbed her home “Villa Maggio” as a tribute to Pvt. Angelo Maggio, the character he portrayed in his Oscar-winning turn in From Here to Eternity (1953).
Ritz studied art and art restoration in Santa Monica and was a designer, collector and animal lover who rescued, cared for or found homes for more than 60 dogs.

“Naomi was funny, charming, strong-willed, wonderfully particular and, at times, challenging,” her daughter said. “Mention an old Hollywood movie, however, and everything could change. She knew the films, the actors and the stories and could play the game of ‘who was in what’ endlessly — and usually win.
“She leaves behind an eye for beauty, a fascination with the past, a house full of stories and collections, an enduring love of animals and a wonderfully individual way of seeing the world.”
Donations in her memory can be made to Bet Tzedek Legal Services or WISE & Healthy Aging, supporting their work to protect older, vulnerable adults from abuse, exploitation and injustice.

title: Juliana Stock Exiting as A+E’s Marketing and Digital Chief to Become Hearst Magazines President
summary: Juliana Stock is leaving her post as president of marketing and digital at A+E Global Media, after more than a decade at the company, to become president of Hearst Magazines.
paragraphs: Juliana Stock is leaving her post as president of marketing and digital at A+E Global Media, after more than a decade at the company, to become president of Hearst Magazines.

Stock’s appointment at Hearst Magazines will be effective Jan. 1, 2027. Debi Chirichella, who has served as president of Hearst Magazines since 2020, will become chair of the group. Stock and Chirichella will report to both Steven R. Swartz, president and chief executive officer of Hearst, and Jordan Wertlieb, EVP and COO.

Hearst Magazines has a portfolio of more than 30 brands in the U.S. — including Cosmopolitan, Elle, Esquire, Harper’s Bazaar and Good Housekeeping — 175 websites and more than 200 magazine editions worldwide. For Stock, it’s a return to the magazine world: Prior to A+E, she worked for 11 years at Condé Nast, most recently as senior director of business and product development.

Hearst’s hiring of Stock comes after it recently tapped another TV veteran for a key position: Chris Berend, previously chief digital officer of the NBCUniversal News Group, who joined Hearst Magazines this summer as chief content and experience officer.

“We welcome Juliana back to the magazine business after more than a decade of leadership positions across digital video, marketing and general management at our A+E Networks,” Swartz said in a statement. “With Debi’s help, she will build on our great brands and great people to lead the next phase of growth in this business in which we have enjoyed a leadership position for more than 100 years.”

Stock said in a statement provided by the company, “Hearst Magazines sets the standard for lifestyle journalism, and I’m honored to join a group with such powerful brands and such a talented team. Audiences are engaging with our content in more ways than ever, including digitally, and there’s a real opportunity to deepen those connections while continuing to deliver the trusted, high-quality print experiences our readers love. I’m grateful to Steve, Jordan and Debi for their confidence and excited to get to work.”

In 2025, Stock was promoted to president of marketing and digital at A+E Global Media. In the role, she led the company’s trade and global consumer marketing, digital strategy and audience engagement initiatives across a portfolio that includes A&E, History, Lifetime, FYI and LMN. Stock is credited with reshaping the company’s marketing approach by realigning operations around “audience-first strategies.”

On the digital side, Stock oversaw the A+E Global Media ecosystem. She led initiatives including the relaunch of History.com, the scaling of direct-to-consumer products (History Vault, Lifetime Movie Club, A&E Crime Central) and the growth of audiences across social platforms and YouTube.

Since joining A+E Global Media in 2013, Stock held senior positions including chief marketing and brand officer. Prior to A+E Global Media, Stock spent more than a decade at Condé Nast, where she helped launch the first websites and iOS magazine apps for Wired, GQ, Vanity Fair and others.

title: Earl Barret, ‘Too Close for Comfort’ Writer and Producer, Dies at 94
paragraphs: Earl Barret, the veteran comedy writer who co-developed the Ted Knight-starring Too Close for Comfort and worked on more than 30 other series, including Bewitched, Get Smart, Batman and The Andy Griffith Show, has died. He was 94.

Barret died Oct. 22 of natural causes at his home in Sherman Oaks, his daughter, J.K. Barret, announced. He was a “lifelong learner with a keen, curious mind and a gift for impeccable comic timing,” she said.
The Ohio native also wrote for My Favorite Martian, My Three Sons, My Mother the Car, I Spy, The Wild Wild West, Julia, The Bob Newhart Show, Sanford and Son and Welcome Back, Kotter.
He and longtime writing partner Arne Sultan developed, wrote and produced Too Close for Comfort, which was based on the British sitcom Keep It in the Family, created by Brian Cooke.

The American adaptation, which ran for six seasons (1980-87) on ABC and in syndication, revolved around Knight’s Henry Rush, a cartoonist who works out of the San Francisco home he shares with his wife (Nancy Dussault) and adult daughters (Deborah Van Valkenburgh, Lydia Cornell).

Barret and Sultan first worked together on the 1969-70 CBS comedy The Governor & J.J., starring Dan Dailey and Julie Sommars. They continued with NBC’s The Partners (Don Adams’ first series after Get Smart), CBS’ The Sandy Duncan Show, ABC’s Holmes and Yoyo and The New Odd Couple and the CTV’s Check It Out (Adams starred on that one, too).
The pair also were among the credited writers on the 1989 feature See No Evil, Hear No Evil, directed by Arthur Hiller and starring Richard Pryor and Gene Wilder.

An only child, Barret was born on Oct. 17, 1932, in Canton, Ohio. His parents, Aurel and Mary, who owned a confectionery store, got him tap dancing and violin lessons as a youngster before the family came west, and he graduated from Hollywood High School and Los Angeles City College.

He originally pursued a career as an actor but changed direction after taking a free TV-writing class taught by Robert C. Dennis, a scribe on shows including Perry Mason and Alfred Hitchcock Presents.
“No matter how busy he was, no matter what show he was working on, he gave a free class every Wednesday night,” Barret noted.
Barret wrote on 1961 episodes of Sea Hunt, Hawaiian Eye and Ripcord, and he and Dennis would later partner on scripts for Get Smart, My Mother the Car, The Andy Griffith Show and The Wild Wild West.

For Batman, he and Dennis came up with the character of King Tut (portrayed by Victor Buono) when producers wanted new villains for the series (the actors playing Joker, Riddler and Penguin apparently were demanding too much money). The duo then wrote the episodes “The Curse of Tut”/“The Pharaoh’s in a Rut” and “The Spell of Tut”/“Tut’s Case Is Shut.”

Barret landed a gig as a story editor on The Governor and J.J., created by Sultan and Get Smart writer Leonard Stern, and before long, he and Sultan were writing for the political comedy. (Barret also directed an episode of the show; later, he would helm 13 installments of Too Close for Comfort.)
Barret and Sultan also wrote the comedy Wife Begins at 40 for the stage, later a 1988 BBC telefilm.
In addition to daughter J.K., survivors include his wife, Barbara; his son, John; and five grandsons. He was preceded in death by another daughter, Lisa.

Barret’s memoir, Eden Was on a Hollywood Hill, was published in 2010. It “tells how a Romanian chauffeur and Hungarian American waitress marry after a one-week courtship and spend the next 50 years pursuing the American Dream through the Great Depression, World War II and finally to the enchanted hills of Hollywood, where they hope their tap-dancing, violin-playing son will break into the movies. And why shouldn’t he? Wasn’t anything possible in America?”

title: Bryan Adams Releases New Trump Protest Song “Lake Ontario”
paragraphs: Canadian rocker Bryan Adams has released another Donald Trump protest song, “Lake Ontario,” included as part of his upcoming album, How’s It Goin.

The single, released to YouTube and other social media platforms by the legendary musician, takes aim at the U.S. president, while never naming Trump directly. A music video for the single has Adams standing on a giant rock alongside Lake Ontario, which Trump renamed as Lake America as part of an executive order amid a tariff and trade war with Canada.

“The lake of shining waters is what the Iroquois called her/ It’s the First Nations name, not an executive order,” assert Adams’ lyrics. The star rocker then insists the lake name change was a diversion from a faltering presidency.

“Things weren’t going his way in Iran/ So like a baby tossing the toys from the pram/ He may have thought it best to throw a low blow/ And create a real dog and pony show/ But it feels like another distraction,” Adams says in his song’s lyrics. “While the Epstein files are getting traction/ One day they’ll come out and we’ll say ‘There you go’ / And then we’ll all dive into Lake Ontario.”

Earlier this year, Adams released another protest song, “51st State,” timed for Canada Day, the nation’s birthday on July 1. That single release followed Trump making repeated taunts about Canada becoming a 51st U.S. state and launching a cross-border tariff war.

Known for timeless hits like ”Summer of ’69,” ”Heaven” and ”Everything I Do (I Do It for You)”, Vancouver-raised Adams has made a name in the global music scene with his love ballads and rock anthems. He was inducted into the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2011 alongside Canada’s Walk of Fame and the Canadian Broadcast Hall of Fame.
His How’s It Goin’ album will be released Nov. 6 via BAD Records. On his website, Adams called the “Lake Ontario” song a response to those looking to rename a perennial cross-border body of water.

“Empires and regimes, dictators and kings, they all come and go. Lake Ontario is forever. This is a song for all the sane people on both shores who know that the current madness will pass, and that Lake Ontario will always be Lake Ontario,” he wrote.

title: Why These 3 ETFs Are a Gentle First Step for a 66-Year-Old Who Owns Nothing but Bonds
summary: A retirement that could stretch 20 or 30 years is a different problem than the one bonds were built to solve, and a 66-year-old sitting entirely in fixed income may be taking on a risk that never shows up on a down day.
paragraphs: Why These 3 ETFs Are a Gentle First Step for a 66-Year-Old Who Owns Nothing but Bonds

A retirement that could stretch 20 or 30 years is a different problem than the one bonds were built to solve, and a 66-year-old sitting entirely in fixed income may be taking on a risk that never shows up on…
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

You’re 66, and every dollar you’ve saved sits in bonds. Maybe you moved there after a bad market shook you. Maybe stocks never felt comfortable. Either way, you built something stable, and that took discipline. The question now is whether that portfolio fits a retirement that could last decades. If you decide to add some stock exposure, three funds offer a measured way in: iShares Core 40/60 Moderate Allocation ETF (NYSEARCA:AOM), Invesco S&P 500 Quality ETF (NYSEARCA:SPHQ), and First Trust Value Line Dividend Index Fund (NYSEARCA:FVD).
Why an All-Bond Portfolio Can Quietly Fall Short

For some retirees, an all-bond portfolio makes sense. If Social Security, a pension, or an annuity already covers your spending, you may not need more growth. Bonds also pay real income today, with the 10-year Treasury yield at 5.00% as of Oct. 26. However, bond funds can still lose value, especially when rates climb.

For everyone else, the risk is quieter than a crash. Over a long retirement, inflation and longevity can slowly eat away at a portfolio that never grows much. Stocks give you a claim on corporate earnings growth, something a fixed coupon can’t provide.

Owning stocks comes with a price. Part of your portfolio will now decline sometimes, occasionally sharply. Go in expecting that, and remember that a rough market in the first few years of retirement does far more lasting damage than one later on (we walked through that sequence-of-returns problem, and how to defend against it, in a free guide here).
How to Start Small and Avoid a Surprise Tax Bill
There’s no need to move a lot or move it all at once. Shift a modest portion, add to it gradually, and see how the swings feel before going further.

Where your bonds live matters. According to the IRS, “Generally, amounts in your IRA, including earnings and gains, aren’t taxed until distributed” (Publication 554). This generally allows you to shift bond holdings inside an IRA without triggering a tax bill at the time of the trade. In a taxable account, selling bonds can realize a gain or a loss, so check before you sell.

AOM is the easiest step because it adds stocks inside a fund that still holds plenty of bonds. Its name signals a 40/60 stock-to-bond mix. As of July 31, 2026, its largest position was a U.S. bond index fund at about 49.6% of net assets, plus an international bond fund at roughly 8.9%. On the stock side, an S&P 500 index fund made up about 23.4%, with international developed markets at 11.7% and emerging markets at 4.4%.

One ticker gets you global diversification and automatic rebalancing. The fund holds roughly $1.74 billion in net assets and pays quarterly, distributing about $1.55 per share over the trailing 12 months. Payouts vary from quarter to quarter.
SPHQ Screens for Financially Sturdy Companies

SPHQ tracks the S&P 500 Quality Index, a subset of S&P 500 companies “determined to have high quality based on return on equity, accruals ratio, and financial leverage ratio.” Translated: profitable businesses whose earnings are backed by cash, carrying manageable debt.

It costs a 0.15% net expense ratio, has operated since Dec. 6, 2005, and manages about $19.4 billion. No single holding topped roughly 5.8% of assets as of July 31, and exposure covers technology, financials, industrials, consumer brands, and health care. It paid about $0.87 per share in quarterly dividends over the past year.
Quality screens don’t prevent declines. SPHQ slipped 0.91% over the past month alone.
FVD Pays Quarterly Income From Safety-Ranked Dividend Stocks

FVD tracks the Value Line Dividend Index, which selects dividend payers that Value Line ranks for safety and that yield more than the S&P 500. The index uses modified equal dollar weighting, so positions sat near 0.4% each as of June 30, 2026. No single company dominates.

You get utilities, insurers, health care, consumer staples, and real estate trusts, plus some international names. The fund holds about $8.04 billion and distributed $1.1225 per share over the trailing 12 months, most recently $0.2562 paid on Sept. 30. Companies can cut dividends, and FVD remains a stock fund that can fall with the market.

Each fund asks you to accept something. AOM’s bond-heavy mix moderates both the swings and the growth, and it can still decline. SPHQ leans heavily on chipmakers and tech names, which can be volatile. FVD’s tilt toward utilities and real estate trusts can lag if rates climb.

Used gradually, these funds let you test stock ownership on your terms: one blended fund that keeps bonds in charge, one that screens for financial strength, and one built around steady dividend payers. For a 66-year-old who owns nothing but bonds, that combination offers a way to add growth potential without giving up the stability you worked to build.

title: Healey provides some breathing space but things still set to get worse for most
summary: The chancellor talked of charting a new course for Britain, but the impact of Iran war has limited his options.
paragraphs: Healey provides some breathing space but things still set to get worse for most
John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.
It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses – and the government's ability to help.
While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain.
The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes.

Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament. On that basis, it could be the second worse parliament for living standards, after the last one, since the 1950s - a sign of how far the war has blown prosperity off course.

But it can't be all be blamed on the war. Taxes haven't helped. Although there were few major measures aimed at households, the policy of previous chancellors of freezing the thresholds at which different rates of tax on income apply - fiscal drag - has been maintained in the background, scooping more money out of pay packets.
Overall, this Budget has the tax burden - the proportion of the nation's income going to the tax office - rising to a new historic high of 38.6%
However, a more generous package of help would have been hard to pull off. The impact of higher inflation and debt have increased borrowing costs by £14bn in the past year alone.
The Chancellor had to prove to the markets which lend the government money that he has a plan to bring down future debt to avoid those costs climbing further.
As it stands, debt interest repayments are due to be £160bn in 2032, more than double the amount spent on schools in England.

And the plans Healey has unveiled already eat into wiggle room he has within the public finances. He says he was right to do so - that's what such safety margins are there for - in times of strife. But the great uncertainty that remains made going further very risky. Energy prices remaining high, for example, could easily chew up all the spare cash.

So the result was what some have termed a beige, safe Budget. As Healey strove to prove his fiscally sound credentials, there wasn't even the customary rabbit pulled out of the hat, the end-of-speech sweetener.
The markets seem reassured – even if some of his tax raising plans involve clamping down on loopholes and those not paying the right tax, which is always highly uncertain.
- Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you
So the chancellor appears to have bought himself some breathing space. But that means some big questions have been postponed until another day, not least on public services.

Higher-than-expected inflation may mean that if areas such as health and defence are prioritised, budgets for some other "unprotected" areas – justice and higher education for example – are set to lag behind inflation after 2028.
There was a hint too from John Healey that he'd tap into some of those budgets to help out defence spending. To maintain those budgets in 2030 would means finding tens of billions of pounds.
And issues around the other big area of spending – welfare – remain unresolved. Between 2025 and 2032, spending there is set to increase by £100bn.

The official forecasters also noted the rapid rise in sickness and disability caseloads since the start of the pandemic. They warn if that trend continued, spending on such benefits would rise by a further £13bn.
Any suggestion of welfare reform has been postponed until the forthcoming review into the plight of workless young people.
Then there's the issue of boosting growth. There was a bit more detail on the plans for devolution – but there is much to be fleshed out.
And on another key part of the growth strategy, housebuilding, there was disappointing news. Even though first-time buyers are set to get more help, their first home may be more elusive.
Between regulation and higher costs – in part, related to the war - the OBR estimates that 190,000 fewer homes will be built by 2032 compared to what it thought in March, a significant setback.
So the chancellor may have unveiled 98 (relatively small) measures but the to-do list gets longer.
With his official forecasters warning that, in a very uncertain world, his finances face exceptional risks, playing a wait-and-see game feels like a prudent move.
The risks go both ways: the OBR points out that a swift resolution to the war and an improvement in the economy could spell a significant boost to the public finances.
So the chancellor has more reason than most to keep his fingers crossed that happens rapidly.
For as it stands, the official forecasters say incomes after inflation, living standards, are set to be only 1% higher at the end of the decade than at the start.
A series of economic shocks outside out control could thwart plans to turbo-boost prosperity . And as today shows, breathing space only extends so far.

title: What Is Behind The Move In Vertiv Stock?
summary: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.
paragraphs: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Vertiv (VRT), the maker of power and cooling systems for data centers, climbed 16.5% on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, outpacing the S&P 500’s 0.3% gain. The advance followed the release of Vertiv’s third-quarter 2026 results. So how strong was Vertiv’s quarter, and what did management say about the rest of the year?
Vertiv Beat Estimates And Raised Its 2026 Outlook

The company easily cleared analyst expectations for both revenue and earnings. Adjusted earnings per share reached $2.21, topping the $1.82 estimate. Revenue totaled $4.31 billion, beating the $3.75 billion estimate, and management said $100 million to $150 million of those sales had been delayed from the second quarter.

Management said customers place orders 12 to 18 months in advance, providing a window into future sales. Vertiv’s organic orders, which exclude acquisitions, increased more than 100% from a year earlier. Management also said it does not plan to share orders figures from now on, so the third-quarter 2026 figure may be the last such number you get.

Management raised its full-year 2026 guidance across all key metrics. The company now expects net sales of $14.7 billion at the midpoint, up $650 million from its earlier guidance, and said on the call that data center demand is accelerating. News reports on October 28 linked the stock’s jump to the results.
Did Eaton, Emerson And nVent Rise With Vertiv?

Eaton, Emerson Electric and nVent Electric, the three peers on the Trefis list for Vertiv, all advanced during the session, but by far less. nVent Electric gained 4.2%, Eaton rose 2.3% and Emerson Electric added 0.9%. The SPDR fund for industrial stocks (XLI) climbed 0.3%, in line with the S&P 500. The peers and the sector fund all posted much smaller gains, so most of Vertiv’s gain was specific to the company.
Where Does Vertiv Stock Stand After The Jump?

Such a large one-day jump is rare for Vertiv. Over the 365 days before the session, the stock posted a gain of at least this magnitude only once: on February 11, 2026, when the stock gained 25%. The most recent move of this size in either direction was a 17.3% fall on July 29, 2026.

Vertiv returned 26.1% over the 12 months to October 28, compared to 14.0% for the S&P 500. The path was uneven. The stock reached its lowest close in that year at $149.83 on December 17, 2025, and its highest was $376.23 on May 14, 2026. Over the six months to October 28, the shares lost 20.6% while the S&P 500 returned 9.1%, and they closed the session well below that May high.
Vertiv is expected to report its fourth-quarter 2026 results in February 2027. Net sales for that quarter are the figure to watch, with management guiding to about $4.4 billion at the midpoint.

After a run like this, the hard questions are personal: hold, trim or sell, and the tax on each. Our partner advisory firm offers a free strategy review of ways to keep part of the upside, protect the rest and spread the tax over years.
Spot an error or want more like this? Tell us in 10 seconds.

title: Why Marvell Stock Is Down Today
summary: Marvell is reportedly close to a massive optics deal, but investors are worried about what it could cost existing shareholders.
paragraphs: Marvell Technology (MRVL -13.78%) stock is sinking, down 13.9% as of 2:44 p.m. ET on Thursday, Oct. 29, after a report said the chipmaker is close to buying a big optics supplier.
The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite were down 0.7% and 1.7%, respectively.

Bloomberg reported after Wednesday's close that Marvell is in advanced talks to acquire Lumentum, a company that builds key optical components for AI data centers. An announcement could land as early as next week according to the report, but nothing has been finalized.

Marvell has about $3.93 billion in cash and equivalents, and given Lumentum's $83 billion market cap, Bloomberg has reported it is likely to be all stock. That means dilution for existing shareholders. The company actually acquired a smaller optics company last year, in a $3.5 billion deal that included $1 billion in cash. This would be substantially larger.

Marvell's overall business is humming, with Q2 revenue up 37% to a record $2.74 billion. I think optics is a smart place for Marvell to grow, but this is a massive deal relative to its size, and whether it pays off is a question we can't really answer until more details come to light.

title: What Just Happened To Celestica Stock?
summary: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.
paragraphs: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Celestica (CLS) shares rose 8.4% on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, outpacing a 0.3% gain for the S&P 500. The advance marked the stock’s second consecutive gain since the company reported third-quarter results on October 26. Peer companies also traded higher that day, with Flex gaining 11.6%. So what did Celestica report?

Celestica reported third-quarter adjusted earnings per share of $3.30, compared with an estimate of $3.02. Revenue reached $5.83 billion, against a $5.40 billion estimate, an 82.5% increase from a year earlier. News reports tied that growth to AI infrastructure demand, with the Compute & Storage division up 242%.

The company said both revenue and adjusted earnings per share finished above the high end of its own guidance ranges. Celestica raised its 2026 guidance and increased its 2027 revenue target to $40 billion, from $35 billion, stating that the 2027 outlook reflects faster revenue growth and a wider adjusted operating margin.
Celestica combined its results call with an investor and analyst day on October 27. News reports linked the shares’ 12.1% rise that day to the results and the raised guidance.

Wednesday’s gain was not limited to Celestica. All five companies on its Trefis peer list rose during the session. Flex gained 11.6% on the day it reported its own quarterly results, while Fabrinet added 7.0%. Flex was the one peer that rose more than Celestica.
The broader technology sector saw much smaller gains, with the XLK SPDR fund rising 0.8%. Celestica climbed alongside its peer group on Wednesday, moving well ahead of technology stocks as a whole.
Celestica Stock Is Still Down Over Twelve Months

You have seen gains this large from Celestica before. The shares rose at least this much in 12 sessions over the prior 365 days, most recently on October 27. Over the twelve months to October 28, the stock lost 0.7%, against a 14.0% gain for the S&P 500.

Within that year, the shares reached a 52-week closing high of $472.40 on June 2, 2026, before dropping to a 52-week closing low of $246.65 on October 26, the day the company reported. The results came out after the close that day, so the low was set before the market saw them. Over the month to October 28, the shares lost 18.2%, while the S&P 500 gained 1.0%.

At Wednesday’s close, Celestica traded at 2.0 times its sales over the past twelve months, against 3.2 times for the S&P 500. Celestica is expected to report its fourth-quarter 2026 results in January 2027, and revenue growth from a year earlier is the figure to watch.

title: Why Is Smurfit WestRock Stock Falling?
summary: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.
paragraphs: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Smurfit WestRock (SW) shares fell 5.2% on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, while the S&P 500 rose 0.3%. The packaging maker posted the decline as it reported third-quarter results that fell short of analysts’ estimates for both earnings and revenue. So what held the quarter back, and what does management now expect for 2026?
What Held Back Smurfit WestRock’s Third Quarter?

News reports said higher costs and weak volumes held the quarter back, linking the miss to freight, energy and raw material expenses. Adjusted earnings came to $0.45 per share, short of the $0.60 consensus estimate, according to Zacks. Revenue reached $8.16 billion, below the $8.29 billion analysts expected.

Management called the cost inflation, mostly in energy and freight, unprecedented and greater than it had anticipated. It said it raised prices across most paper grades to counter those expenses, noting that the increases are passing through with a normal time lag. This means customers pay the new prices some time after the company’s own costs have already gone up.

Management also pointed to one-off events in the quarter, including heat waves in Europe and earthquakes in Colombia. A separate contamination issue in the U.S. agriculture sector hurt the company’s volumes in the United States and Mexico.

News reports noted the company lowered its 2026 outlook as well. Management now expects about $4.7 billion of adjusted EBITDA, its measure of profit before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, for 2026. It said energy costs alone will be about $700 million higher than a year earlier, running materially above earlier expectations. Management did point to demand, adding that corrugated volumes improved from the second quarter and practically all its paper grades remain sold out.
Did Smurfit WestRock Fall With Other Packaging Stocks?

Only partly. Four of the five companies on Smurfit WestRock’s peer list fell alongside it, but three of those peers posted smaller declines than Smurfit WestRock. O-I Glass fell 12.4%, while International Paper rose 3.3%. The materials sector, tracked by the XLB fund, rose 0.2% in the same session, indicating the drop was largely Smurfit WestRock’s own rather than its sector’s.

Declines of this magnitude are uncommon for the stock. Smurfit WestRock registered five sessions with a fall at least this large in the 365 days before this one. Its most recent bigger move in either direction was an 11.1% rise on July 24, 2026.

Over the past twelve months, the stock lost 3.1% including dividends, compared with a 14.0% return for the S&P 500. These losses are recent: the stock fell 14.4% in the three months to October 28, against a 4.4% gain for the index. The $40.33 close sits well below the 52-week closing high of $51.84 set on February 18, 2026, though it remains above the 52-week closing low of $32.79 from November 20, 2025.

Smurfit WestRock is expected to report its fourth-quarter 2026 results in February 2027. When those numbers arrive, full-year adjusted EBITDA, measured against the outlook management gave on the October 28 call, is the figure to watch.

title: Can This Number Push Booking Holdings Stock Higher?
summary: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.
paragraphs: Can This Number Push Booking Holdings Stock Higher?
For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

One group of customers matters to Booking Holdings (BKNG) stock more than it may seem: the top members of its Genius loyalty program. Booking.com may look like a site travelers find through Google, but management says these members return more consistently and book directly more often than travelers outside Genius. Even so, the stock lost 29.0% in the year to October 28, 2026, as the S&P 500 returned 14.0%. So how many of Booking’s room nights do these members book?
Top Genius Members Book Most Of Booking’s Room Nights

Level 2 and Level 3 Genius members made up more than 30% of Booking’s active customers in the June quarter. They accounted for what management called “a high 50% share” of its room nights, and management said on the fiscal Q2 2026 call that both figures were up from a year earlier.

These members also plan their trips further in advance than travelers outside Genius, and management said it sees room to strengthen the Genius offering further. So, as of the June quarter, Booking’s most loyal customers were both a large part of its business and a growing one.
Is Booking Holdings Losing Travelers To AI Search?

Not on the whole, so far. Management said on the fiscal Q2 2026 call that direct room nights kept growing over the four quarters to June, with the direct share of consumer room nights staying in the mid-60% range.
Separately, could Tesla make their product more tangible? See: How Musk’s Massive Marketing Miss Cost Tesla $10 Trillion.

The worry for any online travel company is that AI tools will answer travel questions themselves and send fewer travelers to booking sites. Booking does feel some of that: management said pressure on its traffic from unpaid search results continued in the June quarter, and that Google’s AI overview had probably added to it. But management also said unpaid search remains a small part of Booking’s room nights, and traffic from large language models, paid and unpaid, was still well below 1% of them.

Booking is also putting money into a tool of its own. On October 14, 2026, the company announced a planned $100 million investment in Vayo, its new company offering a personal travel agent that learns how you travel. So far, Booking’s direct business is holding steady as the way people search for travel shifts. Investors are less sure: on September 23, 2026, Booking shares fell with other travel stocks on fears that Muse, Meta’s AI agent, could let travelers bypass booking sites.
Booking Holdings Expects A Slower September Quarter

However loyal its members are, Booking still sells travel, and management guided for slower growth. The company expects room nights to rise between 3% and 5% in the September quarter, against 5% growth in the June quarter. It also expects gross bookings and revenue to rise between 4% and 6%, down from June-quarter gains of 9% and 8%. This guidance assumed that higher flight ticket prices, reduced capacity on some routes and softer long-haul demand, all tied to the Middle East conflict, would last through the third quarter.

Booking’s top Genius members were still gaining share as of the June quarter, and its direct bookings were holding steady. So far, that number backs the loyalty argument for the stock, but it has not kept the stock from falling over the past year. When Booking reports in November 2026, the share of room nights booked by top Genius members and the share of consumer room nights booked directly are the two figures to watch.

title: Why the ECB Rate Hike Cycle Is Not Over
summary: The Iran war, persistent energy inflation and expected second-round inflation effects underscore anticipated further tightening. The challenge for the ECB is to contain inflation without triggering any sovereign debt crisis.
paragraphs: The European Central Bank faces an increasingly uncomfortable choice: risk tightening monetary policy too little as an extended energy shock threatens to entrench inflation, or tighten too much and amplify meaningful strains in sovereign bond markets.

Officials want to prevent the energy crisis from becoming embedded in the regional economy and have left open an option of a hike this week. But for now, the most likely outcome is a hold at the meeting concluding on Thursday, 29 October, with a 25-basis-point rate hike anticipated in December under a quarterly pace of hiking once fresh projections become available.

The Governing Council may begin laying the groundwork for such a December move in its communications this week, even if it stops short of any explicit commitment. The message being that the ECB remains data-dependent, but that the balance of risks has shifted towards inflation running hotter than previously anticipated.

With the Iran war prolonged and energy markets edging beyond even an ECB adverse scenario presented last month, the likelihood of rates being raised above neutral, and staying there for some period after, is becoming harder to dismiss. Further tightening next year can no longer be ruled out.
Inflation's Second Round Is the ECB's Real Concern
The crucial question is if elevated energy prices may increasingly affect domestic price-setting, wage negotiations and inflation expectations.

Headline inflation rose to 3.8% year over year last month (Figure 1) – nearly double a central-bank objective. This is even as core inflation nudged up only one tenth to 2.5%. Nevertheless, the longer headline inflation stays elevated, the harder it becomes to dismiss second-round effects that could make an external shock considerably harder to reverse.
Figure 1. Euro area headline inflation sharply rose last month
Euro area headline and core harmonised index of consumer prices, annual rates of change, %

As I said on Bloomberg – for the ECB, an inflation overshoot is today a far greater medium-run risk than an undershoot. The nominal neutral rate — the rate consistent with the economy operating at its potential without monetary policy pushing demand in either direction — may also be drifting slightly higher from a starting point around 2% as persistent inflation and geopolitical uncertainty reshape the policy backdrop.

The euro should furthermore be watched closely. Its depreciation (Figure 2) adds to the inflationary impulse by making energy and other imports more expensive – amplifying inflationary dynamics and strengthening the case for monetary tightening.

title: What Is Behind The Move In Honeywell Aerospace Stock?
summary: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.
paragraphs: What Is Behind The Move In Honeywell Aerospace Stock?
For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Honeywell Aerospace (HONA) shares rose 5.4% on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, outpacing a 0.3% gain for the S&P 500. The company reported third-quarter results that beat analysts’ estimates for both adjusted earnings per share and revenue, but the release came after the market closed that day, so it did not drive the rise. Two of its four peers on the Trefis list also rose. How big was the beat, and what did management change in its outlook?
Honeywell Aerospace Beat Estimates And Raised Its EPS Forecast

Honeywell Aerospace reported $2.21 in adjusted earnings per share for the third quarter of fiscal 2026, against an estimate of $1.87. Revenue reached $4.64 billion, against an estimate of $4.57 billion. Management said sales grew 2.4% on its organic measure, outpacing its own expectation of flat to slightly higher sales, because mechanical output rose from the previous quarter. It also said a few deals closed earlier than expected, worth about 1 point of growth.

Management said customer demand continued to outpace what its suppliers could deliver. Orders grew in every end market, with Defense & Space and commercial aftermarket up double digits. The book-to-bill ratio, measuring new orders against sales, was 1.3 in the quarter.

Management raised its 2026 forecast for adjusted earnings per share to $7.85 to $8. It credited lower costs below operating profit than it had expected as a new public company. The company kept its forecast for 2026 organic sales growth at 4% to 5%, and said that implies fourth-quarter organic growth modestly below that range. The board also declared the company’s first quarterly dividend of $0.40 a share, payable in December.
Did Honeywell Aerospace Rise With Industrial Stocks And Peers?
Industrial stocks rose far less than Honeywell Aerospace. The SPDR fund for the industrials sector (XLI) gained 0.3% that session, matching the S&P 500.
The four peers on the Trefis list split two and two. NorthStar Earth & Space Enterprises rose 5.7% and Lyntris gained 3.0%, while Firefly Aerospace and Astronics slipped.
Where Does Honeywell Aerospace Stock Stand After The Rise?
Since it began trading on June 29, 2026, Honeywell Aerospace has had three sessions with a rise at least this large. The latest was on August 19, 2026, when it gained 6.0%.

Even after the rise, the shares sit well below their peak. Honeywell Aerospace closed at $177.03 on October 28, against its highest close since its June 29 listing, $247.15 on July 2, 2026. The stock lost 13.4% over the three months to October 28, while the S&P 500 returned 4.4%. That stretch included a one-day fall of 23% on August 6. The past month brought a rebound: the stock returned 13.9%, against 1.0% for the S&P 500.

The company’s next report covers the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026. Organic sales growth for that quarter is the figure to watch, and management expects it to come in modestly below its full-year range.
What Would Another Fall In Honeywell Aerospace Do To Your Plan?

A fall hurts most when one stock is a large part of what you own, and selling it to spread the risk can bring a large tax bill. Our partner advisory firm offers a free strategy review of ways to put a floor under a large position and unwind it with less tax.

title: 'Like cutting up a Picasso': AI microdrama edit of Neighbours worries actors and crew
summary: A micro-drama will use AI-assisted technology to edit old episodes of the Australian TV soap to focus on Margot Robbie's character.
paragraphs: 'Like cutting up a Picasso': AI microdrama edit of Neighbours worries actors and crew
Former Neighbours actors and crew have raised concerns about plans to use AI to help re-edit old footage and make mini episodes for mobile phone viewers.

Fremantle, producer of the now-defunct Australian TV soap opera, has partnered with US-based RoseBerry Media for the project that will use AI to "scan decades of episodes" to help make short vertical videos.
Footage of Margot Robbie, who played Donna Freedman from 2008 to 2011, will be the initial focus of the micro-drama.

Both companies say the move will bring the show - which aired its final episode last year - to new audiences. But some actors and crew say they have not consented to their images, voice or work to be re-purposed.
Robbie has yet to respond publicly. The BBC has contacted her agency for comment.

In a statement, the companies behind the project said the AI-assisted technology will "scan decades of episodes to map character arcs, storylines and standout moments, helping editors quickly identify the strongest material".
The micro-drama episodes will use "original, previously broadcast footage, dialogue and performances", according to Fremantle spokesman.

"It does not generate new scenes or performances, alter actors' faces or likenesses, or use synthetic voices," he said, adding that a human editor would be "reviewing and approving every stage of the editing process".

The mini episodes will likely feature Matt Werkmeister, 34, who joined the set of Neighbours in 2005 when he was 13 years old. He played a regular character, Zeke Kinski and shared many scenes with Robbie's character.
Now a Melbourne-based producer and director, Werkmeister says he hasn't been approached by the companies behind the micro-drama and is concerned what the episodes will feature.
"If they're creating a new micro-drama out of something that already exists, I feel there needs to be consent for using our image and voice as well as the writers," he said.

Robbie is "obviously a big draw card" and "it's nice to watch old clips from shows you used to watch," Werkmeister said, but when he signed his contract two decades ago, "streaming didn't even exist as a platform" so he's unsure of what his rights are.
That uncertainty is also at the forefront of Sam Clark's mind. He played Ringo Brown on Neighbours from 2006 to 2010, a character who later marries Robbie's fictional character.
Speaking from Los Angeles, Clark – now working as a producer and voice actor - said he hadn't heard about the micro-drama until a friend sent him an article.
"I don't have a negative view of the work that we did all those years ago getting a second life as long as it's not being manipulated into new storylines," Clark, 39, said.
"AI and social media obviously wasn't a thing when I signed my contract 20 years ago so I'm still trying to understand exactly what those parameters are."
Sound recordist Bruce Findlay, 68, has worked in the TV industry for close to five decades and Neighbours has a "special place" in his heart, having worked on the show from episode one.
Using AI to help make short episodes from old footage was "like cutting up a Picasso and rebuilding it".
"We worked so hard to get this product out… and now they're chopping it up into little tiny pieces, throwing it up in the air and putting it back together again using AI - it belittles the process".

Guy Hameiri, head of RoseBerry Media, said the project is the first time the company will use its in-house AI tool to sift through Neighbours footage - there are more than 9,300 episodes - to make "premium vertical television".
The project will "reimagine" the material, giving it "new audiences, new relevance and new value," he said.
The head of Fremantle's commercial and international arm, Jens Richter, has called the project "an exciting example of how technology and creative thinking can unlock new value" from their catalogue.

It's understood that Fremantle is in discussions with two unions on the issue and that residuals - ongoing payments for actors and writers when their work is re-aired or syndicated - will be paid, but this does not apply to crew.
The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance, one of the unions, confirmed the talks.
"Workers should be consulted before their likeness or expertise is used in a way they could never had envisioned when they signed contracts decades ago," said MEAA's acting CEO Adam Portelli.
